text:
Permitting reform negotiators finally landed their big deal. Now comes the hard part.

By punting a vote until after the election,senators opened October to fierce lobbying from all sides. They’ll also have to navigate a volatile lame-duck session, where shifts in power could reshape everyone’s incentives.

Senate Environment and Public Works CommitteeRanking Member Sheldon Whitehouse(D-R.I.) pushed that door open further by vowing to put together a manager’s amendment, meaning the bill could change before it reaches the floor.

And Democrats are still working to finalize a side agreement with the White House over President Donald Trump’s blockade on wind and solar projects.

Several industry groupsfrom across the spectrum — from clean energy, to oil and gas, to manufacturing — have come out in support of the bill, which was negotiated by an interesting mix of progressive and conservative senators.

“I am pretty stoked about this,” Rep. Scott Peters (D-Calif.) said in an interview. “We have a really good working document on paper that is supported by members of the Senate literally from the left and the right, and we’ll get similar support in the House.”

That breadth of support will help negotiators who feel like they pulled off a difficult balance: easing approvals for all types of energy projects to meet rising power demand while still preserving communities’ right to weigh in.

“That’s what made this actually a really fun negotiation because there’s value across the board even in stuff that other people brought to the table,” a senior GOP aide involved in negotiations said.

But landminesare already emerging.

What’s next? The utility sector is likely to push for changes to provisions giving the federal government more power to site interstate lines that carry clean energy across the country, including a significant expansion of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s backstop siting authority.

Utilities, whose political clouthas faded somewhat as electricity costs have skyrocketed, could also fight mandatory language requiring data center developers to cover associated grid costs. That provision is stronger than the voluntary Ratepayer Protection Act, which Democrats blocked.

“We are nervous about what if the utilities start to whack away at the good parts?” one environmental and clean energy advocate told us. “As long as it stays where we think, it is a net positive for the ratio of clean energy. We will find a way to support it.”

Environmentalists are expected to contest a provision that would sharply limit courts’ ability to remand or vacate agency decisions under NEPA. Language narrowing Section 401 of the Clean Water Act — a top White House priority aimed at stopping blue states from blocking pipelines — could also draw scrutiny, though some Democrats argue it could help interstate transmission lines too.

The House is another obstacle. Rep. Jared Huffman(D-Calif.), ranking member of the House Natural Resources Committee, said progressives would hold out for more next Congress if Democrats win big on Election Day. Conservatives are also likely to resist rubber-stamping a Senate-led permitting overhaul.

name: Detroit and Evs
title: The EV Bet's Hidden Bill: GM Can't Build the Cars Buyers Want
description:
GM spent about $390 million to retool Fairfax for the next-generation Bolt EV.
Toyota sold what GM refused to build While GM retooled, its competitors sold.
GM “has only the electrified Corvette.” “Consumers are interested in hybrids and GM can’t compete,” Cox Automotive senior economist Charlie Chesbrough told Bloomberg.
We said so in 2013, 2014 and 2024 NLPC has warned GM about this for more than a decade.
GM tore out a car people bought to build one they wouldn’t buy.
text:
In 2024, General Motors shut down production of the Chevy Malibu at its Fairfax plant in Kansas to make room for a battery-powered car. By 2027, that EV will be gone from Fairfax too, replaced by a gas-powered Chevy Equinox.

That round trip, from gasoline to battery and back, shows why American car buyers are walking into showrooms this fall and finding almost nothing new.

The industry has hit a dry spell for fresh designs

Automakers are expected to redesign just 9% of their lineups across the 2026 through 2028 model years, well under the 20-year average of 14%, according to analyst John Murphy. The Wall Street Journal found this week that new entries are sparser now than after the pandemic shutdowns or the 2007-09 auto crisis.

“We’re in a total stall for new products,” Murphy said.

The Journal traced the drought to one source. The billions carmakers poured into electric vehicles “diverted time and money from the types of models that buyers crave today, from hybrids to V8-powered trucks.”

Buyers never wanted EVs in the numbers Detroit planned for. Demand fell short, the paper said, then plunged when Washington ended subsidies and clean-air mandates last year. The world’s automakers have since scrapped or delayed dozens of EV models and booked more than $70 billion in charges, and GM’s share has climbed to $10.9 billion.

The writedowns were only the first bill. The second is arriving now, in lost years.

Fairfax went from gasoline to battery and back again

When GM announced the Malibu’s end in May 2024, the family sedan had sold 130,300 units the year before. GM spent about $390 million to retool Fairfax for the next-generation Bolt EV. In January 2025 the gas-powered Cadillac XT4 also left the plant to clear space for the Bolt.

The Bolt started rolling off the line in November 2025. Two months later, Electrek wrote that GM would bring in the gas Equinox in 2027 and the Buick Envision in 2028, and that once the Bolt run ends, “only internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles will be made at the facility.”

Two gas nameplates out, one EV in, and then the EV out. Each switch costs months of retooling and a new supply chain.

“This industry does not turn on a dime,” a Stellantis spokesman told the paper. Most of the new vehicles Detroit is now rushing to build won’t reach dealers before 2028.

Toyota sold what GM refused to build

While GM retooled, its competitors sold. The paper found that GM and Ford lost market share this year to Toyota, Honda and Hyundai, which “have more hybrids and lower-cost offerings.”

With gas near $4 a gallon, Toyota offers hybrids on more than 20 U.S. models, Bloomberg reported in June. GM “has only the electrified Corvette.”

“Consumers are interested in hybrids and GM can’t compete,” Cox Automotive senior economist Charlie Chesbrough told Bloomberg.

GM’s first plug-in hybrids aren’t due until 2027. When chair and CEO Mary Barra announced them in 2024, she explained they would help GM “comply with the more stringent fuel economy and tailpipe emission standards.” Regulators, not shoppers, set the timetable.

Cox analyst Erin Keating told the Journal that Detroit is missing out on hybrids and affordable models, segments where Asian rivals with broader lineups don’t have to wait for new arrivals to meet demand.

GM does earn one concession. Murphy’s industry number would be lower still without its redesign of its top-selling pickups. The trucks, which GM never abandoned, are the part of the lineup that works.

Cadillac dealers are stuck with a six-year-old flagship

The luxury brand shows the damage at its sharpest. In 2021, Cadillac’s then-global vice president Rory Harvey told CNBC, “We will not be selling ICE vehicles by 2030.” Cadillac stopped developing new gas-powered entries and began retiring the ones it had.

The three-row XT6 ended production in 2025. It had sold 20,225 units in 2024, while its electric replacement, the Vistiq, managed 7,879 in 2025, according to Jalopnik. In July, Cadillac said the gas XT6 would return.

Michael DiFeo, a New Jersey Cadillac dealer, told the Journal the Escalade hasn’t seen a major redesign in more than six years. His customers have noticed.

“I literally have people saying, ‘I am not leasing this car again. It’s the same car and the price keeps going up,'” DiFeo said.

Cox’s Keating described the bind for sellers: “You want to show the value of a price increase.” Without a new design, a dealer has nothing to show.

We said so in 2013, 2014 and 2024

NLPC has warned GM about this for more than a decade. In February 2013, we quoted Toyota vice chairman Takeshi Uchiyamada’s verdict that the electric vehicle “is not a viable replacement for most conventional cars.”

In January 2014, as Barra prepared to take the top job, we noted that Toyota’s Prius outsold GM’s Volt and Spark EV combined by about ten to one. “If Ms. Barra’s vision for GM truly centers on plug-in electric vehicles,” we wrote, “there will be a price to pay.” That February, Cadillac sold just 58 of its plug-in ELRs.

By 2015, even Volt champion Bob Lutz acknowledged that carmakers were “trying to recover what they’re losing at the other end with what I call compliance vehicles.” The people paying for those losses were buyers of conventional trucks and SUVs, the kind of customers DiFeo now hears complaining about higher prices on aging designs.

In 2024, we urged GM shareholders to have the board reconsider executive pay tied to the EV program, warning that the strategy “may not align with genuine market demand or economic viability.” The board opposed it.

GM tore out a car people bought to build one they wouldn’t buy. Next year, it tears that one out too.

title: Merz touts green technology's growth potential, calls for international carbon markets
description:

text:
Chancellor Friedrich Merz has stressed the importance of Germany’s green technology sector for the country’s economic future, pointing to innovation in renewable energy production and energy efficiency as key elements of his government’s sustainability strategy. “Sustainability is key to answering the questions of the 21st century,” Merz said at the annual conference of the German Council for Sustainable Development (RNE) in Berlin on Tuesday (29 September).

The chancellor said that Germany’s green technology sector has grown at an average rate of five percent a year over the past 15 years, meaning it has doubled in value since 2010 and greatly surpassed overall economic growth. “It is therefore counterproductive to constantly say that there is an almost insurmountable target conflict between climate action and economic growth,” Merz said, adding that sustainable technologies rather have a “complementary” relationship with economic growth and today include some of the most dynamic global markets.

Germany generated more than 300 billion euros in gross value added in the green technology sector in 2023, which Merz said could account for up to two percent of the country’s overall GDP in the coming years. A push on innovation in the government’s “High-Tech Agenda” would seize this momentum and include more support for technologies in clean mobility and nuclear fusion, Merz noted.

The government’s latest Sustainability Action Programme, a set of cross-sectoral measures that aim to bring about progress on the UN’s sustainability targets that the government adopted on Wednesday (30 September), would aim to ensure that sustainability measures enjoy broad acceptance and quickly turn into benefits for citizens, he added.

Merz said Germany’s leading position in many green technologies mean the country has the chance to shape the next stage of industrial development towards greater sustainability. “The transformation towards climate neutrality will pay off in the long run,” he said, arguing that the state’s most important task in this respect is to set reliable guidelines to let market forces work.

An international market for carbon emissions that can be processed with carbon capture and storage or usage (CCS/CCU) would be a logical next step to complement carbon pricing that allows European companies to regain competitiveness, the chancellor said. Creating such a market would become possible once more countries become convinced of the growth prospects of climate neutral technologies. “And that is currently happening,” Merz said.

name: Clean Energy
title: Clean Energy Manufacturing & Supply Chains – Themes & Focus Areas
description:
India's renewable energy transition is increasingly being supported by a rapidly expanding domestic manufacturing ecosystem.
Alongside becoming one of the world's largest renewable energy markets, the country is also emerging as a major manufacturing destination for solar, energy storage and clean energy technologies.
The most significant progress has been witnessed in solar manufacturing.

India's renewable energy transition is increasingly being supported by a rapidly expanding domestic manufacturing ecosystem. Alongside becoming one of the world's largest renewable energy markets, the country is also emerging as a major manufacturing destination for solar, energy storage and clean energy technologies.

The most significant progress has been witnessed in solar manufacturing. Supported by the ₹24,000 crore Production Linked Incentive (PLI) Scheme for High Efficiency Solar PV Modules, India's solar module manufacturing capacity has increased from approximately 2.3 GW in 2014 to around 203 GW as of July 2026. During the same period, solar cell manufacturing capacity has grown from around 1.2 GW to approximately 32 GW, representing one of the fastest manufacturing expansions globally.

India is also strengthening upstream capabilities across the solar value chain. The commissioning of the country's first integrated ingot-to-wafer manufacturing facilities marks an important milestone towards reducing import dependence and creating a more resilient domestic manufacturing ecosystem. Policy measures such as the Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM) and Quality Control Orders have further strengthened quality standards and supply chain reliability.

As global demand for clean energy technologies continues to grow, India is positioning itself as a competitive manufacturing hub capable of serving both domestic and international markets while creating jobs, strengthening industrial competitiveness and enhancing energy security.

description:
Tariffs raise electricity prices and reduce social welfare Under a tariff-free regime, electricity typically flows from Canada’s IESO and HQ into the NYISO system.
This study provides an empirical, quantitative evaluation of how geopolitical interventions in the form of electricity tariffs can directly affect power system operations in North America.
However, during periods of elevated natural-gas prices, Canadian imports remain cost-competitive and continue to clear in the market.

The implications of electricity tariffs depend on the objective used to assess policy coherence.
text:
Canadian imports supplied about 10% of NYS’s total load

NYISO maintains interconnections with four Regional Transmission Organisations and Independent System Operators (RTOs/ISOs), including cross-border interties with Ontario’s Independent Electricity System Operator (IESO) and Quebec’s Hydro-Quebec (HQ), as well as domestic interties with the PJM Interconnection (PJM) and ISO New England (ISO-NE) (Fig. 1a).

Monthly interchange data from 2015 to 2024 (Fig. 1b) indicate that NYISO primarily imported electricity from IESO, HQ, and PJM, while exporting modest volumes to ISO-NE during non-summer months. Net imports typically supplied 10–20% of NYISO’s total load. Focusing on Canadian interchanges (Fig. 1c), NYISO remained a consistent net importer until late 2023, when drought-driven declines in Quebec’s hydropower output, wildfire-related infrastructure disruptions, and falling natural gas prices reversed the flow, temporarily turning NYISO into a net exporter to HQ. To meet system demand under these conditions, NYISO relied increasingly on supplemental imports from PJM.

IESO and HQ can export up to 2,500 megawatts (MW) and 2,100 MW, respectively, to NYISO. Between 2015 and 2024, Canadian imports accounted for 9.89% of NYISO’s load, including 4.25% from Ontario and 5.64% from Quebec. Although Canadian imports accounted for a modest share of annual load, they supplied more than 30% of instantaneous demand in 0.02% of five-minute intervals and reached a maximum of 45% (Fig. 1d). At an hourly resolution (Fig. 1e), Canadian imports exceeded 20% of NYISO’s total load in 0.56% of hours (492 h over the decade).

Tariffs raise electricity prices and reduce social welfare

Under a tariff-free regime, electricity typically flows from Canada’s IESO and HQ into the NYISO system. Both entities generally maintain surplus low-carbon generation capacity and export competitively priced electricity to NYISO, with HQ relying primarily on low-cost hydropower and IESO drawing mainly from nuclear, hydro, and wind resources. These imports allow NYISO to reduce dependence on higher-cost in-state fossil-fuel generation. Cross-border electricity trade yields mutual economic benefits13: Canadian suppliers gain export revenues, while NYISO consumers access more affordable power.

To quantitatively evaluate the impacts of import tariffs on market-clearing dynamics, we analyse NYISO’s publicly available day-ahead market bidding data (2015–2024), comprising roughly 165 million records submitted by in-state generators, load-serving entities, and interregional traders. A tariff-adjusted marginal supply–demand equilibrium model (Supplementary Methods) is used to simulate market outcomes under tariff scenarios. Here, the tariff term represents an incremental trade cost on Canadian electricity delivered into NYISO, covering both a U.S. import tariff and a Canadian export surcharge, as either measure raises the effective offer price of affected import bids. Two sets of scenarios are evaluated: tariffs imposed solely on imports from Ontario and tariffs applied to imports from both Ontario and Quebec. Sensitivity to tariff magnitude is assessed across a range of tariff levels, including a complete-curtailment scenario in which Canadian imports are completely curtailed.

Tariffs alter both cross-border electricity imports and marginal energy prices (MEPs) in NYISO. By eroding the cost advantage of Canadian RTOs/ISOs, tariffs reduce daily imports as rates rise (Fig. 2a–b), while MEPs increase in parallel (Fig. 2c–d). However, during certain hours, Canadian imports continue to clear despite tariffs because alternative supplies are limited or more expensive. Neighbouring RTOs/ISOs have limited capacity to supply additional electricity at competitive prices, forcing NYISO either to rely on more expensive in-state generation or to continue importing Canadian power despite the tariffs. Complete curtailment during these hours produces larger increases in simulated MEPs, as shown in Fig. 2c–d.

When tariffs are applied solely to imports from Ontario, IESO’s market share falls to a low level once the tariff exceeds roughly 55% (Fig. 2a). Beyond this threshold, further increases in tariff rates have little additional effect on import volumes or market prices (Fig. 2a, c). In contrast, when tariffs are extended to both Ontario and Quebec, the threshold rises to about 90% (Fig. 2b, d), reflecting HQ’s stronger cost advantage from low-cost hydropower resources. These thresholds are estimated from historical NYISO day-ahead bidding and market-clearing data over 2015–2024, and therefore reflect the natural gas prices, load levels, renewable generation availability, import availability, and other system conditions prevailing over the historical sample.

Although Canadian electricity is typically cost-competitive, import tariffs incentivize a shift toward in-state generation and alternative imports from other RTOs/ISOs, particularly from PJM (Fig. 2e–f; Supplementary Fig. 3). At the same time, rising market prices suppress demand, especially among price-sensitive loads whose bids fail to clear the market. These changes produce distinct distributional welfare effects, as shown by the waterfall decomposition in Fig. 2g–h; enlarged versions are provided in Supplementary Fig. 4. The welfare-reducing components include losses to NYISO load, which faces higher marginal energy prices and reduced access to lower-cost Canadian electricity, and losses to Canadian exporters facing tariffs, whose tariff-adjusted bids become less competitive. The welfare-increasing components include gains to NYISO generators, substitute exporters from other neighbouring RTOs/ISOs, and trade-charge revenues collected by the relevant government, either as U.S. import tariff revenues or as Canadian export-surcharge revenues. However, these gains do not fully offset the losses. The net welfare effect is negative, corresponding to deadweight losses from tariff-induced reductions in mutually beneficial cross-border electricity trade. These welfare effects may also spill over to neighbouring markets. Qualitatively, reduced exports from tariff-affected Canadian provinces can leave more electricity available for local consumers and potentially lower local prices, while increased exports from substitute neighboring RTOs/ISOs may tighten their own supply–demand balances and put upward pressure on local prices. Thus, tariff-induced welfare redistribution can propagate through interconnected RTOs/ISOs, producing broader cross-regional impacts beyond the NYISO market.

Time-series analysis of monthly average MEPs and import volumes (Fig. 2i–l) shows that Canadian import volumes respond differently to tariffs over time, as reflected in the simulated changes in cleared imports after tariff-adjusted bid prices are incorporated into market re-clearing. Because marginal generation in NYISO is predominantly gas-fired, fluctuations in natural-gas prices are the primary driver of MEPs. Correlation analysis further shows that the relationship between natural-gas prices and MEP increases strengthens as tariff rates rise, whereas the correlation between natural-gas prices and import reductions remains high and relatively stable across tariff levels (Supplementary Fig. 5). These patterns suggest that Canadian imports help stabilise the system by diversifying the supply mix, particularly during periods of elevated fossil-fuel generation costs. In winter, when heating demand tightens regional gas supply, Canadian import volumes become less responsive to tariffs, as alternative supply from in-state gas-fired generators and neighbouring U.S. RTOs/ISOs becomes more expensive. For example, in early 2015 and 2022, approximately 70% of baseline Canadian imports persisted even under a hypothetical 100% tariff (Fig. 2k–l). In contrast, during periods of low gas prices, Canadian import volumes become more responsive. These results indicate that Canadian interconnections contribute to supply availability and moderate price increases during periods of elevated gas prices. A stratified analysis by natural-gas price range further confirms this pattern, showing that the tariff threshold for Canadian import reductions rises under higher gas-price conditions (Supplementary Note 2 and Supplementary Fig. 6).

Tariffs increase emissions and affect progress toward climate targets

NYS has established statutory climate targets under the Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act (CLCPA)14, including sourcing 70% of its electricity from renewables by 2030 and achieving a zero-emission grid by 2040. Low-carbon imports from Canada contribute to progress toward these targets15, as most of the imported power is low-carbon. HQ’s generation portfolio is approximately 99% renewable, dominated by hydropower, and produces virtually no direct emissions. Similarly, electricity from IESO is largely sourced from nuclear, hydro, and wind generation, with fossil fuels accounting for only about 12% of total output in recent years.

Changes in imports (Fig. 2e–f) are used to estimate the resulting shifts in the fossil and non-fossil components of Canadian electricity imports (Supplementary Methods and Fig. 3a–b) for the period 2018–2023. Tariffs constrain NYISO’s access to low-carbon electricity from IESO and HQ, thereby increasing reliance on in-state fossil generation and raising net imports from PJM and ISO-NE. At lower tariff levels, where export reductions are limited, IESO reduces gas-fired generation while continuing to fully utilise its hydropower capacity. In contrast, at higher tariff levels, larger export reductions lead to underutilization of surplus hydropower in the IESO’s system.

These shifts in the generation mix translate into corresponding changes in emissions, since each megawatt-hour displaced from Canadian imports is effectively replaced by higher-emission generation within the U.S. These impacts are quantified using the annual average emissions intensity of fossil-fuel generation for each RTO/ISO (Supplementary Methods), reflecting the fact that marginal generation in NYISO, PJM, and ISO-NE is predominantly fossil-fuelled. As a result, tariffs not only reduce reliance on clean Canadian electricity but also increase fossil-fuel consumption and greenhouse-gas emissions in the U.S. Changes in emissions under each tariff scenario are attributed to individual RTOs/ISOs and presented in Fig. 3c–d. Figure 3e–f reports the associated increases in NYISO power purchase costs under the tariff scenarios. Combined with the emissions increases shown in Fig. 3c–d, these results show that electricity import tariffs are economically and environmentally dominated by the tariff-free baseline, increasing both electricity procurement costs and CO₂-equivalent emissions by restricting access to low-carbon Canadian imports.

Maintaining open cross-border interconnections yields benefits beyond direct emissions reductions from low-carbon Canadian imports. Quebec’s hydropower reservoirs function as large-scale, dispatchable energy-storage systems16,17,18, with an estimated capacity of 175.5 terawatt-hours (TWh)19, and can provide flexibility to support the integration of variable renewable energy in NYS20. This flexibility is particularly important for achieving the state’s CLCPA target of 70% renewable electricity by 2030, which will require wind and solar deployment as well as storage to balance temporal mismatches between supply and demand21. Realising these benefits depends on deeper cross-border grid integration and investment in high-capacity, bidirectional transmission corridors5,22, which could reduce reliance on more costly in-state storage infrastructure23,24. However, electricity import tariffs create long-term policy and revenue uncertainty for such investments. For example, the 1,250 MW Champlain Hudson Power Express (CHPE), a project costing approximately 6 billion U.S. dollars (USD) and connecting Quebec to New York City, entered commercial operation in May 2026 under financing and contractual assumptions of tariff-free cross-border trade. Introducing tariffs after commercial operation could reduce revenue certainty under long-term power-purchase arrangements, alter expected congestion and energy-market revenues, and increase perceived policy risk for future cross-border transmission projects. Such uncertainty could deter investment in cross-border transmission infrastructure that supports clean-energy integration and delay progress toward NYS’s CLCPA emissions and climate targets.

Open grid interconnections support grid reliability

Cross-border electricity flows increase geographic diversity and operational flexibility, which can support system reliability25. NYISO’s interconnections with IESO and HQ provide additional flexibility for load balancing and contingency response. For the NYISO power system, summer and winter are the most vulnerable seasons. In summer, NYS reaches its annual peak electricity demand, tightening supply margins and necessitating the start-up of costly oil-fired generators to meet peak-hour loads. In winter, severe storms can cause unplanned generation outages that may lead to system-wide load shedding. To quantify the reliability contribution of Canadian electricity imports during summer peak-load hours and severe winter storms, a data-driven assessment is conducted using historical NYISO operational data. The NYISO transmission system is modelled using publicly available datasets and historical records, incorporating key components such as transmission lines (Fig. 1a and Methods), generation units (Fig. 4a), and spatially disaggregated load profiles (Fig. 4b and Supplementary Methods).

During summer peak-load hours, import tariffs reduce simulated system reserve margins. As imports from tariff-affected Canadian RTOs/ISOs decline, additional imports from other neighbouring RTOs/ISOs are re-estimated under the tariff-adjusted market-clearing model and capped by the available transfer capability of each external interface; these imports only partially offset the shortfall, increasing reliance on in-state generation and thereby reducing reserve margins across the NYISO system. These effects are evaluated through summer stress tests covering the 100 most severe peak-load days, primarily in July and August. System operations are simulated using a day-ahead unit commitment model coupled with real-time single-contingency (N − 1) security checks (Supplementary Methods), capturing generator dispatch under observed weather, load, and import conditions across multiple tariff scenarios. The day-ahead model produces hourly generation schedules, while the real-time model further evaluates their feasibility under N-1 security conditions. Results show sharper reductions in transmission flows during peak hours when exports from both Ontario and Quebec are curtailed, compared with Ontario-only reductions (Fig. 5a). The associated redistribution of in-state generation is shown in Fig. 5b. Additional transmission-flow and generation-distribution results under varying tariff rates are provided in Supplementary Fig. 7. Stress tests further show that curtailing Canadian imports reduces the daily minimum reserve margins of gas-fired units (Supplementary Fig. 8), forcing reliance on local oil-fired peakers to maintain required reserves and regulation capacity, particularly under high-tariff or cutoff scenarios. Limited access to Canadian imports increases the dispatch and simulated capacity factors of local oil-fired peakers during peak-load stress tests (Fig. 5c). These units have historically operated infrequently and generally have higher operating costs than commonly dispatched generation resources. Reliance on these resources increases operating costs and dependence on units with limited suitability for sustained operation.

During the simulated winter-storm contingencies, Canadian imports provide additional generation and reserve support, particularly during contingency conditions. This is evident during Winter Storm Elliott (23–26 December 2022), which caused load shedding in the Eastern Interconnection due to freezing issues, fuel shortages, and mechanical or electrical failures26 (Supplementary Note 3). Winter-storm scenarios are simulated under varying levels of power support from Canada (Supplementary Methods). Generation outages are assumed to occur only among gas-fired units, identified as the most vulnerable based on reports from Winter Storm Elliott26. System reliability is evaluated using metrics that quantify the magnitude and duration of both load and reserve deficits, defined as instances when available reserves fall below required levels (Fig. 6 and Supplementary Fig. 9). Results show that full, real-time-responsive electricity support from Canada reduces unserved energy and load- and reserve-deficit hours in the NYISO system under simulated winter-storm outages, including scenarios with a 50% gas-unit fault rate. In contrast, complete suspension of Canadian imports increases modelled unserved energy, load-deficit hours and reserve-deficit hours.

Beyond regular seasonal peaks, projected growth in artificial intelligence (AI) data-centre demand may increase electricity consumption in NYS, reduce reserve margins, and increase ramping requirements27,28. This evolving demand landscape reinforces the importance of interregional interconnections that can supplement supply and provide rapid ramping support during system stress.

This study provides an empirical, quantitative evaluation of how geopolitical interventions in the form of electricity tariffs can directly affect power system operations in North America. Historical operational data for NYS are combined with an empirical simulation framework to quantify the impacts of trade barriers on cost efficiency, emissions, and reliability within a physically interconnected regional grid.

Simulation results based on historical bidding records from NYISO’s day-ahead market reveal that tariffs on Canadian electricity imports reduce their cost advantage, particularly for low-carbon hydropower and nuclear resources. This advantage is closely tied to regional natural gas prices that largely determine the marginal cost of in-state generation. When tariffs exceed 55% for Ontario-only imports and 90% when applied to both Ontario and Quebec, Canadian electricity is nearly priced out of the market. However, during periods of elevated natural-gas prices, Canadian imports remain cost-competitive and continue to clear in the market. In their absence, the system becomes increasingly reliant on in-state fossil generation, resulting in higher marginal electricity prices and a measurable decline in social welfare. These distortions not only reduce overall market efficiency but also impede climate progress: clean imports are displaced by higher-emission domestic generation, which increases CO₂ emissions and power purchase costs, especially during periods of fuel price volatility.

Tariffs also reduce reserve margins in the summer stress tests and increase expected unserved energy and load- and reserve-deficit hours in the winter-storm simulations. During simulated summer peak periods, Canadian imports increase reserve availability and reduce the dispatch of oil-fired peaking units. This effect is particularly evident for Quebec’s high-voltage interties, which deliver electricity directly to transmission-constrained downstate zones, including New York City and Long Island. Reductions in HQ exports therefore increase localised supply deficits and the need for higher-cost in-state generation. In winter-storm simulations based on the 2022 Winter Storm Elliott, full, real-time-responsive support from Canada raises the modelled gas-unit failure threshold at which load shedding begins from 40% to 55%, indicating the contribution of responsive cross-border support during system contingencies.

Taken together, the results indicate that Canadian electricity imports reduce modelled costs and contribute to operational reliability and clean-energy objectives in NYS. As trade-based interventions pose increasing policy risks, preserving open and tariff-free electricity trade can support a reliable, cost-effective, and low-carbon grid.

The modelled results suggest that electricity-trade policy could consider potential effects on cross-border market coordination and system operation. Electricity occupies an unusual position in trade agreements because it combines features of a traded energy product and a network service, while key activities such as transmission access and system operation remain shaped by domestic regulation29. Although electricity trade generally improves cost efficiency and reliability, its benefits depend on compatible market rules and coordinated system operation; incomplete integration across different regulatory regimes can itself introduce inefficiencies30. In the modelled scenarios, tariffs add a trade distortion, reduce mutually beneficial transactions, and weaken reliability and decarbonization outcomes. A bilateral energy security protocol could require consultation with system operators before imposing restrictions.

Imports support resource adequacy and provide additional supply during emergencies, particularly in the face of extreme events. Tariffs that restrict electricity flows reduce reserve margins and limit the capacity for coordinated response. Policy frameworks should therefore support the continued operation of interconnections across national boundaries and safeguard operators’ ability to provide mutual support without undue political constraints. Cross-border contingency planning could further improve system reliability and flexibility.

Long-term infrastructure investment in cross-border transmission requires renewed commitment. Projects such as the CHPE can contribute to an affordable, reliable, and low-carbon electricity supply. To reduce investor risk, governments could provide guarantees or insurance mechanisms to mitigate exposure to trade policy uncertainty. Using electricity cooperation as a platform for climate diplomacy reinforces the principle that U.S.–Canada integration enhances energy security, economic competitiveness, and the clean-energy transition for both countries.

Trade policy should be evaluated against explicit energy and climate objectives. The implications of electricity tariffs depend on the objective used to assess policy coherence. Tariffs on Canadian electricity may be consistent with an agenda that prioritises domestic U.S. generation. Yet for jurisdictions pursuing power-sector decarbonization, clean-energy mandates, and regional reliability, they work in the opposite direction. By penalising low-carbon and flexible Canadian hydropower and nuclear-rich imports, tariffs shift dispatch toward higher-cost and more carbon-intensive domestic resources, undermining New York’s CLCPA targets and broader regional decarbonization efforts31,32. Policy coherence for clean-electricity systems, therefore, requires trade rules that preserve access to low-carbon imports.

This study is subject to several limitations, primarily stemming from limited access to real-world data due to security and commercial sensitivity. Because NYISO bidding data are anonymized, tariff impacts are inferred from marginal variations around historical clearing prices rather than from a full market-clearing model, which may introduce bias. In addition, the state’s detailed transmission network model is not public. The synthetic network, reconstructed from multiple open sources, may deviate from the actual transmission network. These limitations could be mitigated with access to more comprehensive datasets.

text:
Daily Briefing: US energy permit reform | Glacier melt ‘explosion’ | Brazil election

News

US senators hit deal on energy project permitting bill, vote seen after November

Timothy Gardner and Nichola Groom, Reuters

US senators have reached a deal to reform laws on the permitting of large energy and infrastructure projects, reports Reuters. The news outlet says the bill, set to be voted on after the US midterm elections, aims to “speed up federal approvals by setting deadlines for environmental reviews, limiting court challenges and making it harder for permits to be overturned once issued”. It also “places emphasis on the electric grid, creating ​new processes for approval of ​transmission lines and upgrades” and “includes provisions to accelerate renewable energy projects and explicitly covers both onshore and offshore wind”, according to the newswire. The Associated Press reports that the bill would “ensure AI data centres are forced to pay for the increased electricity they use and would mark a significant change to a landmark environmental law [the National Environmental Policy Act] that critics say slows the process of building energy projects”.

The New York Times says the Trump administration has announced that South Korea would invest up to $200bn in power projects in the US, including a gas plant in Texas, eight nuclear power plants and a liquefied natural gas (LNG) facility in Alaska. The Hill notes that South Korea is committing $54bn toward the Alaska LNG project, which it notes is an 807-mile pipeline that would carry natural gas from Alaska’s north slope to the southern part of the state for export to Asian markets. It adds that the “project has faced years of questions over its cost and commercial viability”. Reuters notes South Korea’s investment package is “designed to secure critical exemptions from punishing US import tariffs”. The Financial Times, Le Monde and CNBC also cover the energy deal.

MORE ON US

Politico says US president Donald Trump is still considering a diesel export ban to bring down prices, despite “fierce pushback from the oil and gas industry”. The Times notes that the administration has briefed UK officials about possible disruption to diesel supplies.

The Financial Times: “US oil industry warns diesel prices will not return to normal for a year.”

Senate Democrats blocked legislation intended to offset the impact of data centres on consumer electricity bills, according to the Guardian.

The Associated Press: “Senate punts bill to permanently ban Chinese cars until after midterm elections.”

The Hill and Reuters look at the upcoming Supreme Court case brought by Suncor Energy and ExxonMobil against Boulder, Colorado. Reuters says the case could “determine the fate of dozens of ​climate-related lawsuits by state and local governments against fossil-fuel companies”.

Power use by electric vehicles in the US is increasing at the slowest pace in at least three years, according to Bloomberg.

Africa’s richest man launches Kenya oil refinery despite land protests

Nkechi Ogbonna, Waihiga Mwaura, Peter Mwangangi and Ondiro Oganga, BBC News

Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote and Kenya’s president William Ruto have broken ground on a $16bn oil refinery in Lamu Kenya’s northern coast, reports BBC News. Upon completion, the refinery is expected to process 700,000 barrels of crude oil a day, making it East Africa’s “largest industrial project by capacity”, according to the news outlet. BBC News notes that protests from local residents demanding compensation for land used for the refinery ahead of the launch were dismissed in an interview by Dangote as “games played by local marketers and international players”. The Financial Times notes the refinery is going ahead after a court delayed the launch over a dispute. Specifically, the newspaper adds that the court ordered “the status quo prevailing” be maintained at the site until a hearing in October. Reuters says the project is “aimed at lowering East Africa’s fuel costs” but “faces opposition from environmental campaigners, who fear it could affect Lamu old town, a world heritage site hosting fragile marine life”.

UK regulator abandons mandatory climate disclosures for listed companies

Phoebe Seers, Reuters

The UK Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) has dropped plans to require listed companies to inform investors about ​their climate risks, after firms raised concerns about implementation ‌costs and competitiveness, reports Reuters. FCA proposals in January set out plans to require listed companies to meet a new UK climate standard, which covered ​climate-related risks and opportunities, climate targets ​and the potential impact of climate change on their ⁠business, according to the newswire. However, the article notes that final rules allow companies to instead maintain a “comply ​or explain” approach. The newswire adds that the move comes after the EU took steps to “water down” its flagship corporate climate disclosure regime and the US “ditched plans for ​any rules”. The Financial Times similarly notes that regulators have been “retreating from strict climate reporting requirements”. While such rules had been seen as “key to helping investors and lenders gauge the risks from climate change”, they have been “called into question” since Trump was re-elected, reports the newspaper.

MORE ON UK

The Guardian covers a report that finds UK banks are Europe’s “biggest coal financiers”.

The Daily Telegraph reports that UK prime minister Andy Burnham said he would look at measures that could reduce high energy costs this winter.

The CEO of energy company EDF has urged Burnham to greenlight the Jackdaw and Rosebank fossil-fuel projects, according to the Daily Telegraph. Meanwhile, the boss of the Offshore Energies UK trade group said approving the projects would amount to “climate leadership”, reports DeSmog.

Green party leader Zack Polanski has written to foreign secretary Ed Miliband, asking him to block development of the Rosebank oil field over the project’s ties to Israel, according to the Daily Telegraph.

In a story trailed on its frontpage, the Daily Telegraph says the UK’s “diesel crisis” is “expected to deepen” after the country’s biggest refinery shuts for “up to 10 weeks”.

Two million people in the UK are “unaware” of the flood risk to their properties, according to the Guardian.

‘Explosion of melt rates’: 20% of Swiss glaciers lost in five years

Ajit Niranjan, The Guardian

The Guardian is among a raft of outlets to cover an annual monitoring report from Swiss glacier monitoring service Glamos which finds the country has lost almost one-fifth of its ice in just five years. The newspaper adds that Swiss glaciers “shrank by 5.5% in the first eight months of 2026…after a summer of scorching heatwaves that followed a winter with little snow”. It says that this reduction in ice volume “falls just shy of the record set in 2022 and brings the total loss of glacier ice since 2021 to 19.4%”. The Associated Press covers a statement from Glamos and the Swiss Academy of Sciences which said: “Alpine glaciers have no chance of surviving in the long term under such conditions”. It also quotes Glamos’ Matthias Huss as saying: “The warming that we are experiencing now can be attributed 100% to anthropogenic climate change. It’s as simple as that.” BBC News and Reuters also cover the research.

MORE ON CLIMATE CHANGE

The Guardian covers a report from the EU’s Copernicus climate change service that found a record-breaking 23 zettajoules of heat was sunk into the oceans last year.

India has recorded its lowest monsoon rainfall in more than a decade, according to Reuters.

Sea levels off southern California are expected to begin rising by half a foot or more and then stay elevated for months, as an enormous pulse of wave energy generated by El Niño travels up the coast, reports the Guardian.

El Niño has stymied storm formation in the north Atlantic “even more than expected”, says Scientific American.

The Guardian looks at how El Niño-driven wildfires are “overwhelming” Indonesia’s orangutan population.

China extends two trade-barrier probes into US until December 2027

Shi Bu and ​Liz Lee, Reuters

China’s commerce ministry has decided to extend two probes into US trade practices that “disrupt global ⁠supply and industrial chains” and “hinder trade in green products” by three months until December, reports Reuters, citing a statement issued by the ministry. The newswire adds that the announcements came days after China and the US agreed to a “two-month extension of their trade truce” through to January and tariff cuts on $60bn of ⁠products. State news agency Xinhua says that the two probes were launched in March this year. text:
Gateway Fleets has placed a follow-on purchase order for 200 Workhorse W56 all-electric step vans, building on the 100 W56 trucks it ordered earlier in 2026. Workhorse Group and dealer Kingsburg Truck Center announced the order this week. Gateway is buying the vans through Kingsburg and plans to lease them mainly to independent last-mile package delivery providers. Deployments are expected to begin in the second half of 2027.

Highlights

200 W56 step vans in the follow-on order, after Gateway’s initial 100-truck W56 order earlier this year

Deployments expected from the second half of 2027, continuing through 2028

210 kWh battery, 150-mile nominal range, 10,000-lb payload, and 1,000 cubic feet of cargo space

More than 1,100 vehicles delivered to date by Workhorse, with over 21 million real-world miles, according to the company

How Does Gateway’s Lease Model Work?

Gateway Fleets is a California-based provider of electric vehicle and charging packages for commercial delivery operators. Its model bundles electric trucks with charging infrastructure, fleet support, and depot access under flexible financing arrangements.

Under the lease structure, operators get the fuel and maintenance savings of electric vehicles while managing cash flow and avoiding large upfront capital costs, the companies say. Gateway currently runs depots in Southern California and is expanding its network to meet operator demand across the region and beyond.

For Workhorse, the order widens a sales channel to delivery operators looking for a lower-barrier route to fleet electrification.

“In today’s era of high and volatile fuel prices, customers are seeking the stability and lower operating costs associated with electric trucks, without sacrificing safety or performance,” said Scott Griffith, Chief Executive Officer at Workhorse. “We believe Gateway’s innovative model will help unlock wider adoption of electric trucks through its bundled pricing that eliminates the two biggest barriers to widespread adoption: the higher upfront cost of the vehicle and the added investment capital required to build out the charging infrastructure.”

W56 Specifications for the Gateway Order

The W56 step vans offered through Gateway use a single configuration:

Wheelbase: Standard Wheelbase (178 inches)

Battery: 210 kWh

Cargo space: 1,000 cubic feet

Payload: 10,000 lbs

Nominal range: 150 miles per charge

Each van has an integrated composite body and an ergonomic driver environment, on a platform Workhorse says is engineered for high-cycle last-mile delivery.

Deployment Timeline and Production

The new vehicles are scheduled to begin deploying in the second half of 2027, so customers can put them into fleetwide service before the holiday “peak” season, when package delivery volumes spike. Deployments are expected to continue through 2028.

Gateway is adding W56 trucks as it opens new sites.

“Getting the truck on the road is only the beginning. Keeping operators moving takes the right combination of infrastructure, service, and support,” said Jamie Miller, Chief Revenue Officer of Gateway Fleets. “Workhorse has brought us an innovative vehicle and a team committed to standing behind it, while Kingsburg provides the service expertise and support our customers need in the field. Gateway brings those pieces together with the charging infrastructure and capital to make electrification work for operators. As we open new locations, we’re continuing to expand W56 deployments alongside our network, with more sites and trucks coming online through ‘peak’ and into 2027. We’re excited to keep building on what’s working together.”

Workhorse builds all W56 models at its manufacturing facility in Union City, Indiana. The company says the plant can produce more than 5,000 vehicles per year on a standard operating shift.

Kingsburg Truck Center’s Role

Kingsburg Truck Center is the dealer on the transaction. It handles sales, incentive processing, and service support.

“This partnership brings together three critical components of fleet electrification: a high quality, proven Workhorse truck; a deployment and service partner, Gateway; and our team at Kingsburg, providing full-circle consultative sales, incentive processing and service support,” said Jerry Smith, Owner at Kingsburg Truck Center. “We’ve had nothing but positive feedback on the performance of the W56 this year, and we’re looking forward to an even better 2027.”

title: Regulators Release a Plan to Help Repair the Contaminated Roanoke River
authors: Derek Harrison, Lisa Sorg, Johnny Sturgeon
description:
The plant occupies 2,400 acres at the confluence of Welch Creek and the Roanoke River, where logs are turned into absorbent materials used in diapers and other paper hygiene products.
For 50 years, Domtar’s predecessor, Weyerhaeuser, discharged toxic dioxins, furans and mercury—byproducts of the bleaching process—into the Roanoke River.
Federal and state regulators have now reached a tentative agreement with Domtar to restore and protect natural areas in the Roanoke River watershed.
“Residents of Plymouth and downstream communities deserve a healthy and clean Roanoke River,” said North Carolina Secretary of the Environment Reid Wilson.
Donate Now More than 200 bird species live or breed in the Roanoke River floodplain, among them yellow-throated vireos, American redstarts and cerulean warblers.
text:
PLYMOUTH, N.C.—Fall had just arrived when a nor’easter began stewing in the Atlantic Ocean, its gale-force winds carrying the pungent smell of chlorine westward, away from downtown. Against the backdrop of dingy stratus clouds, the Domtar pulp mill loomed.

The plant occupies 2,400 acres at the confluence of Welch Creek and the Roanoke River, where logs are turned into absorbent materials used in diapers and other paper hygiene products. But those goods come at an environmental cost.

For 50 years, Domtar’s predecessor, Weyerhaeuser, discharged toxic dioxins, furans and mercury—byproducts of the bleaching process—into the Roanoke River. Scientists have found dioxins in river sediment, wood duck eggs and fish.

Federal and state regulators have now reached a tentative agreement with Domtar to restore and protect natural areas in the Roanoke River watershed. A federal court has issued a proposed consent decree and restoration plan to correct the damage that Weyerhaeuser caused.

Although Domtar isn’t responsible for the original damage, the company assumed liability for the cleanup after buying the property from Weyerhaeuser in 2007.

Fish can absorb dioxin through their gills. The contaminant accumulates in the fatty tissues of larger, predatory fish that rank higher on the aquatic food chain. Large fish eat smaller, bottom-feeding species that have consumed even tinier, contaminated organisms.

Since 1990, dioxin levels in and near the river have declined, but state health officials still recommend limiting consumption of car and catfish caught there to no more than one meal per month.

Even at very low levels, dioxin can cause reproductive and developmental problems, damage the immune system and cause cancer, according to the World Health Organization. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency has set limits for dioxin in drinking water and requires facilities to report their releases as part of their pollution permits.

In addition to the toxic dioxin discharges, state records show Weyerhaeuser withdrew water from the river as part of the manufacturing process. Those withdrawals killed larval fish by inhaling them into cooling tanks, reducing the total number of striped bass, river herring and white perch by 100,000 each day, state and federal records show.

The Nature Conservancy in North Carolina owns and protects about 2,000 acres near Domtar. The group is reviewing the draft restoration plan and plans to submit comments, said Julie DeMeester, Freshwater and Coastal Plains director.

The Roanoke River boasts the largest intact systems of bottomland forests on the Atlantic Coast, as well as diverse populations of diadromous fish—species that travel between fresh water and salt water.

The river’s last 137 miles, which include the segment that passes Domtar, are exceptional habitat, DeMeester said, which prompted the Nature Conservancy to begin protecting the lands in 1982.

“There are many imperiled fish that use this river,” DeMeester said. “It’s truly one of the wildest remaining rivers,” with floodplains as much as five miles wide in the lower basin.

“Residents of Plymouth and downstream communities deserve a healthy and clean Roanoke River,” said North Carolina Secretary of the Environment Reid Wilson. “This settlement ensures protection of fish and wildlife habitat, abundant recreational opportunities and strengthened resilience to flooding.”

Domtar did not respond to a request for comment, but issued this statement to WCTI, a television station in New Bern: “We are aware of the consent decree that has been filed and reserve further comment until the public comment period is concluded and the decree is ordered.”

The Roanoke is often overshadowed by its more well-known river peers, the Neuse and the Cape Fear, but it is equally important. The Roanoke begins in the Blue Ridge Mountains of Virginia and squiggles for 410 miles before it empties near Plymouth into the Albemarle Sound, among the largest estuaries in North Carolina.

Donate Now

More than 200 bird species live or breed in the Roanoke River floodplain, among them yellow-throated vireos, American redstarts and cerulean warblers. The river supports one of the most diverse fish communities in North Carolina, including striped bass, alewife and Atlantic sturgeon, which is on the endangered species list.

“It’s a lifeblood for North Carolina,” said Larry Baldwin of the North Carolina Environmental Advocacy Corps, a new nonprofit group.

The Importance of the Roanoke

Pulp and paper mills, as well as the chemical and metals industries, routinely discharged dioxin into waterways until the late 1980s, when the EPA National Dioxin study found the contaminant in fish and sediment. Those findings prompted the federal and some state governments to more closely regulate dioxin releases.

Dioxin releases have fluctuated over the last decade. Most emanated from the chemical industry, while pulp and paper mills accounted for less than 1 percent.

In 2024, Domtar released 3 grams of dioxin into waterways, a third of the state’s total, EPA data show. Dioxins are measured in grams because they are usually produced in very small quantities; they are also toxic at much lower concentrations than many other chemicals.

The Weyerhaeuser site in Plymouth was so contaminated that the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency considered it eligible for the Superfund program, based on its hazard score. However, since Domtar has been willing to pay for the cleanup, the site is being remediated under the Superfund Alternative Approach, which does not require federal funds.

Weyerhaeuser excavated contaminated material from the landfill and former chlorine plant before Domtar purchased the property in 2006, EPA records show. Since 2011, Domtar has spent at least $5.5 million on remediation. That includes installing a thin cap of sand to contain contaminated sediment in Welch Creek.

Baldwin, of the N.C. Environmental Advocacy Corps, said his group’s mission is to monitor overlooked river basins, including the Roanoke, Chowan and others in the northeastern part of the state, as well as environmental justice communities. Census data show two-thirds to 90 percent of residents living in neighborhoods near the Domtar plant are people of color.

The area has more than 50 hog CAFOs, including two that produce swine gas, and an unknown number of poultry operations. Enviva’s wood pellet plants in the region have been linked to deforestation. Much of the Albemarle Sound, which receives water from the Roanoke, Chowan and Alligator rivers, is on the federal list of impaired waters.

“The Roanoke is the major player when it comes to impacts to the Albemarle,” Baldwin said.

“We can’t neglect the importance of that river.”

text:
Two years ago this week, Hurricane Helene’s floods nearly wiped out the little downtown of Marshall, North Carolina, about 20 miles north of Asheville. Situated along the French Broad River, an art gallery, coffee shop, restaurant, and other beloved community spaces were left without water or electricity — half-demolished and caked in mud. They closed their doors for months while they rebuilt. Some are still recovering.

But the Beacon of Hope Food Pantry was spared. The nonprofit is a five-minute drive from Main Street and higher in elevation — safe from the river that rose a historic 27 feet that day.

“We were one of the lucky ones,” said Jessi Koontz, executive director for Beacon of Hope, which has been in operation for nearly 30 years and provides food assistance to 1,700 families in Madison County each month. ​“We had water. We had power. And there was one small puddle in the corner of our thrift store.”

After the deluge, Koontz and many on her team did what they always do: gather resources and serve people in need. They wrestled with guilt over their good fortune, but they also realized, Koontz said, ​“If we had all lost everything, no one would be here to help in the recovery.”

When the inevitable next storm blows through, Beacon will be even better prepared to help its community. It has just installed a microgrid with 56 rooftop solar panels and three batteries, which can store electrons when the sun is shining and discharge them at night or on cloudy days. The system can power the internet, lighting, and heating, cooling, and refrigeration in the pantry’s food distribution area.

“It’s so great,” Koontz said. ​“It’s a $100,000 project, and Beacon has paid nothing.”

That’s because the food pantry received funds from a $5 million state grant program established last summer to install 24 sustainable microgrids in Helene-impacted counties.

“It is the first site we’ve gotten this far,” said Sara Nichols, energy and economic development manager at Land of Sky Regional Council, a local government organization and a lead ally in the state initiative. ​“This was one of the first sites that was selected. It ranked really high, given its community placement.”

Beacon’s solar array is not the only clean microgrid in the region — far from it. In the days after Helene, the nonprofit Footprint Project teamed up with Land of Sky, the North Carolina Sustainable Energy Association, green tech companies, and others to pool donations and set up dozens of them everywhere they could — from fire stations to nursing homes to mobile home parks.

The partnership endured and expanded after blue skies returned, with more climate tech installed seemingly every week, thanks to in-kind donations and an array of private grant and loan programs.

But Beacon’s rooftop solar and battery system is unique because it is financed almost entirely by the state. Last August, the administration of Gov. Josh Stein, a Democrat elected in 2024 who has prioritized Helene recovery, announced it was allocating funds from the Biden-era bipartisan infrastructure law to set up the microgrid initiative, in collaboration with Land of Sky and area nongovernmental organizations.

State officials have been advertising the program and taking applications for months. Beacon will be the first — or possibly the second, depending on exactly when it flips the switch on its solar array — to make it all the way through the process. A microgrid at Bill’s Creek Community Center in Lake Lure, another small town devastated by Helene, about 70 miles southeast of Marshall, is also close to completion.

The two projects are furthest along in part because they’re small and their wiring is relatively simple. While Nichols and the selection committee have drawn interest from plenty of larger, more complex microgrids, those necessitate foreign components that don’t comply with Biden-era rules for federally funded infrastructure. The Department of Energy can waive those rules on a case-by-case basis, but the process is time-consuming.

The wrinkle means the state initiative, which is scheduled to wrap up by next summer, is shifting focus away from more complicated microgrids to ones like those at Beacon and Bill’s Creek, Nichols said. ​“Our projects will trend smaller and more rural — and there are still a lot of outstanding options.”

In Beacon’s case, the state is the biggest but not the only financier. BuildUS, a philanthropic foundation aimed at speeding the transition to a cleaner and more equitable economy, chipped in. Invest Appalachia, a regional fund for economic development, provided a bridge loan. While nonprofits can earn federal rebates to cover 30% of solar installations, it can take over a year for them to get that money back.

“A lot of nonprofits don’t have $27,000 of cash on hand — or whatever the amount — to make these projects happen. A lot of for-profits don’t either,” said Lauren Sowers, director of communications and impact for Invest Appalachia. ​“We’re really just trying to make that timing gap for reimbursement work.”

With the microgrid in place, Beacon will be more resilient in the face of the next storm, even a minor one. ​“It doesn’t take a Helene to have a power-grid failure in rural western North Carolina,” Sowers said. ​“Even those brief outages can have a huge impact.”

The panels will also save the nonprofit money. Over the course of an average year, the solar panels will shave at least a quarter off Beacon’s electric bill, netting it some $5,600 to reinvest in alleviating food insecurity — a problem that became more acute last summer when the Republican Congress sharply curtailed federal food assistance.

“Programs were being defunded left and right,” Koontz said,” and we saw a 50% increase in the number of families seeking food.”

That surge in need prompted Beacon to relocate its thrift store last year to free up more room for food distribution. She and her team found a place for rent on Main Street, giving the nonprofit a small role in revitalizing downtown Marshall.

“[The storefront] was only available when we were looking because it had been completely washed away during Helene,” she said. ​“They were just finishing up the remodeling, and we had perfect timing.”

After Helene, Koontz is clear-eyed about extreme weather in western North Carolina, once thought of as a climate haven. ​“We now know that hurricanes in the mountains are possible,” she said. ​“Our world is changing in some very scary ways.”

text:
Much will happen in the auto industry over the next four years, including the reclassification of vehicles for the US market, based on new, less-stringent corporate average fuel economy standards announced this week. Starting in model year 2030, the US Department of Transportation wants vehicle classifications to reflect reality, eliminating a decades-old loophole that allowed many popular vehicles – ranging from the massive Chevrolet Suburban to the old Chrysler PT Cruiser to be labeled as light trucks.

What sounds like a bizarre, wonky policy crafted for corner cutting to evade environmentally focused fuel-efficiency mandates since the 1970s has actually altered the US market in unforeseen ways, while doing little to improve air quality or vehicle affordability.

So Many 'Light Trucks' Without Beds

For instance, sedans have been disappearing from the US market, and some automakers say it's because consumers want bigger vehicles instead. But in truth, federally regulated CAFE standards are much more stringent for unibody sedans, coupes, roadsters, hatchbacks, and wagons – the so-called passenger cars – while literally every other vehicle type – from Chrysler minivans and Chevy Equinox crossovers to full-size body-on-frame Ford Expeditions and F-150 pickups – is considered a light truck for federal purposes in regulating fuel economy and emissions.

Of course, certain automakers lobbied for that change long ago and continue doing so today because profit margins are commensurate with vehicle size. All this explains why the average price of a new car in America hovers around $50,000 and why Ram and Jeep are Stellantis' two most robust brands in the US.

The Department of Transportation says the new rules will accurately reflect a vehicle's purpose. It's not clear whether it's actually stated in the standards, but perhaps a "truck" will need a bed, or at least more room for cargo than people.

More Hatchbacks, Wagons Coming?

If these rules actually roll out in 2030, the department says automakers will no longer be "disincentivized from making hatchbacks, wagons, and smaller footprint vehicles in general." But analyst Sam Abuelsamid is skeptical that more hatchbacks and small cars are on the way.

"I don't expect any changes in the short term, but three to five years out we could see some shifting back to cars — although it might be limited," says Abuelsamid, vice president of Telemetry Insights.

"Automakers like pushing the crossovers because they get higher margins on them, and margins are always a challenge on small cars."

–Sam Abuelsamid, VP of Telemetry Insights

While the new rule is intended to eliminate incentives for automakers to add equipment for a crossover SUV to be considered a light truck, for instance, Abuelsamid says most of these vehicles don't actually have that much more equipment than a comparable car, beyond a higher seating position. "Basically, if an OEM says it's a light truck, it's a light truck," even without additional equipment, he says. The current Buick Envista and the old Chevy HHR were all considered light trucks.

Focus On Off-Road Capability Will Remain

On the other hand, dedicated off-road variants such as Honda Trailsport, Toyota Woodland, and Hyundai XRT models actually do get more rugged equipment, he says. "Given the popularity of these variants, I don't see automakers backing away from them," Abuelsamid says.

While the new rules seemingly open the door to more full-size SUVs and pickup trucks without fear of federal penalties or fines, Abuelsamid doubts that will happen, partly because they are expensive and consume lots of fuel while gasoline prices spike. For the record, Abuelsamid says profit margins on big trucks and SUVs are typically between $15,000 and $20,000 – and even higher for variants like Raptor and TRX.

"I don't actually expect large truck/utility sales to climb significantly because the market is getting saturated, and market share has stayed flat in the 18-20 percent range since the early 1980s."

–Sam Abuelsamid

Efficiency Necessary For Affordability

Despite these relaxed fuel-economy regulations fitting neatly into President Trump's push for deregulation on many fronts, Abuelsamid expects automakers will continue developing more efficient vehicles to remain competitive and improve affordability. "The only way to improve affordability is make the vehicles cheaper to operate," he says. "They also have to be ready to compete against the Chinese at some point, so nothing is really going to change."

Hybrids, battery-electric vehicles, and extended-range EVs will remain in automaker product plans because "it helps reduce the total cost of ownership, which helps affordability in the absence of lower prices," Abuelsamid says, noting the cost premium for hybrids has shrunk dramatically. Again, these alternative powertrains will be necessary to compete with China, he says.

CarBuzz Insight – Why This Matters:

By 2030, the Transportation Department expects the new CAFE regulations will cut the average cost of a new vehicle in the US by $1,300, and that the current fleet mix of 70% light trucks and 30% passenger vehicles will flip the other way, to around 70% passenger vehicles.

Closing loopholes is a good idea, and it makes sense to reclassify vehicles based on how they are actually used or even constructed, for instance, body-on-frame versus unibody. A key question remains about compliance and enforcement, as the Trump administration has said it won't issue any fines. But after 2029, a future administration could decide to retroactively fine companies for non-compliance.

text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Senators from both parties said Wednesday they have reached a deal on legislation aimed at speeding up permitting reviews for new energy and infrastructure projects that now face yearslong delays, as lawmakers seek to meet growing demand for electricity and other forms of energy.

The bill, proponents argue, would cut down the arduous timeline for getting big energy projects off the ground at a time when demand is rising because of mushrooming data centers for artificial intelligence. The bill would ensure AI data centers are forced to pay for the increased electricity they use and would mark a significant change to a landmark environmental law that critics say slows the process of building energy projects.

Republican Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia, chair of the Environment and Public Works Committee, called the bill “a major step toward making it faster and more efficient and easier to build infrastructure projects” of all types while maintaining important environmental protections.

Vote on the bill won't happen until after the midterms

“The American people sent us here to do big things. This is a big thing. It’s monumental and it’s legacy-setting,” Capito said at a news conference at the Capitol where she was joined by Republican Sen. Mike Lee of Utah and Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island. The four senators lead the chamber's energy and environment panels.

Heinrich said the bill “will mean more energy on the grid, more good-paying jobs, and lower electricity costs for families and businesses. And as data centers drive demand for more power, it will ensure they pay their fair share of the grid upgrades they require — not leave that bill to American families.”

A vote on the bill won’t happen until after the midterm elections — reflecting the fraught political reality as elections loom that could change partisan control of both chambers. But the bill represents a rare instance of bipartisanship over the country’s energy policy as lawmakers from both parties agree on the need to build new energy projects of all types.

Lee, who chairs the energy committee, said he is confident the bill will be approved in a lame-duck session in November, noting its bipartisan support and encouragement from business and environmental groups.

Whitehouse, the top Democrat on the environment panel, also was hopeful but said Democrats were still seeking clarity on how the bill will prevent President Donald Trump's administration from blocking wind and solar projects.

He and Heinrich, the top energy Democrat, have decried what they call Trump's “reckless and vindictive assault on wind energy” that includes repeated actions to block large-scale wind projects under construction off the East Coast. The administration suspended five offshore wind projects in December, citing unspecified national security concerns.

The projects later moved forward after federal judges intervened. A federal judge also struck down Trump’s executive order blocking wind energy projects early in his second term.

Brad Campbell, president of the Conservation Law Foundation, an environmental advocacy group, panned the deal, saying it “appears to adopt a fossil fuel industry wish-list.” He said the bill could roll back protections for clean water and endangered species, limit judicial review and curtail the power of the Environmental Protection Agency and states to consider impacts of energy projects.

Drew Maloney, president and CEO of the Edison Electric Institute, which represents for-profit utilities, said he was encouraged by provisions to streamline environmental permitting and “create project certainty.” The group is reviewing the transmission provisions to see how they affect efforts to deliver electricity to its 250 million customers, he said.

In a statement, the White House said the bill would “deliver transformative policies to lower Americans’ energy and housing costs, drive new construction and investment in American infrastructure, and create American jobs.”

Trump's wind opposition played a role in delaying a deal

Trump's opposition to wind power has been a consistent stumbling block to a deal on permitting reform, which Democrats say can only go forward if the administration agrees to allow previously approved projects to move forward.

Trump recently offered to ease his administration’s holdup on renewable energy projects, in part to entice Democrats to agree to a permitting deal. But it was unclear how long the offer would last and whether it would change after the election results are known.

Whitehouse called the administration's proposal reasonable but said the overall issue remains “unresolved.”

Manish Bapna, president and CEO of the Natural Resources Defense Council, said his group was studying the bill’s details, but said: “Ensuring the agreement puts an end to the Trump administration’s war on clean energy — the cheapest and fastest sources of energy — will be a necessary element to any deal.”

Capito was confident such obstacles can be overcome.

Both parties recognize that for far too long, “America has had a permitting system filled with delays, expenses, red tape, uncertainty,'' she said. “Too long, too expensive. And we’ve seen projects that should be finished more quickly (take) decades” to complete.

The Senate bill would limit legal challenges under the National Environmental Policy Act, a bedrock environmental law that requires federal agencies to consider a project’s possible environmental impacts before it is approved. The law has increasingly been blamed for stalling projects of all types.

Challenges under the National Historic Preservation Act also would be restricted. The law protects Native American cultural treasures and other important artifacts.

The bill would ease siting of interstate transmission lines and strengthen the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s authority to review major projects at the same time as state reviews, helping needed projects move through the overall permitting process more quickly.

The bill also would require data centers to pay for all associated transmission costs, preventing costs from being passed on to families or businesses.

___

Associated Press writer Jennifer McDermott contributed from Providence, R.I.
