text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Senators from both parties said Wednesday they have reached a deal on legislation aimed at speeding up permitting reviews for new energy and infrastructure projects that now face yearslong delays, as lawmakers seek to meet growing demand for electricity and other forms of energy.

The bill, proponents argue, would cut down the arduous timeline for getting big energy projects off the ground at a time when demand is rising because of mushrooming data centers for artificial intelligence. The bill would ensure AI data centers are forced to pay for the increased electricity they use and would mark a significant change to a landmark environmental law that critics say slows the process of building energy projects.

Republican Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia, chair of the Environment and Public Works Committee, called the bill “a major step toward making it faster and more efficient and easier to build infrastructure projects” of all types while maintaining important environmental protections.

Vote on the bill won’t happen until after the midterms

“The American people sent us here to do big things. This is a big thing. It’s monumental and it’s legacy-setting,” Capito said at a news conference at the Capitol where she was joined by Republican Sen. Mike Lee of Utah and Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island. The four senators lead the chamber’s energy and environment panels.

Heinrich said the bill “will mean more energy on the grid, more good-paying jobs, and lower electricity costs for families and businesses. And as data centers drive demand for more power, it will ensure they pay their fair share of the grid upgrades they require — not leave that bill to American families.”

A vote on the bill won’t happen until after the midterm elections — reflecting the fraught political reality as elections loom that could change partisan control of both chambers. But the bill represents a rare instance of bipartisanship over the country’s energy policy as lawmakers from both parties agree on the need to build new energy projects of all types.

Lee, who chairs the energy committee, said he is confident the bill will be approved in a lame-duck session in November, noting its bipartisan support and encouragement from business and environmental groups.

Whitehouse, the top Democrat on the environment panel, also was hopeful but said Democrats were still seeking clarity on how the bill will prevent President Donald Trump’s administration from blocking wind and solar projects.

He and Heinrich, the top energy Democrat, have decried what they call Trump’s “reckless and vindictive assault on wind energy” that includes repeated actions to block large-scale wind projects under construction off the East Coast. The administration suspended five offshore wind projects in December, citing unspecified national security concerns.

The projects later moved forward after federal judges intervened. A federal judge also struck down Trump’s executive order blocking wind energy projects early in his second term.

Brad Campbell, president of the Conservation Law Foundation, an environmental advocacy group, panned the deal, saying it “appears to adopt a fossil fuel industry wish-list.” He said the bill could roll back protections for clean water and endangered species, limit judicial review and curtail the power of the Environmental Protection Agency and states to consider impacts of energy projects.

Drew Maloney, president and CEO of the Edison Electric Institute, which represents for-profit utilities, said he was encouraged by provisions to streamline environmental permitting and “create project certainty.” The group is reviewing the transmission provisions to see how they affect efforts to deliver electricity to its 250 million customers, he said.

In a statement, the White House said the bill would “deliver transformative policies to lower Americans’ energy and housing costs, drive new construction and investment in American infrastructure, and create American jobs.”

Trump’s wind opposition played a role in delaying a deal

Trump’s opposition to wind power has been a consistent stumbling block to a deal on permitting reform, which Democrats say can only go forward if the administration agrees to allow previously approved projects to move forward.

Trump recently offered to ease his administration’s holdup on renewable energy projects, in part to entice Democrats to agree to a permitting deal. But it was unclear how long the offer would last and whether it would change after the election results are known.

Whitehouse called the administration’s proposal reasonable but said the overall issue remains “unresolved.”

Manish Bapna, president and CEO of the Natural Resources Defense Council, said his group was studying the bill’s details, but said: “Ensuring the agreement puts an end to the Trump administration’s war on clean energy — the cheapest and fastest sources of energy — will be a necessary element to any deal.”

Capito was confident such obstacles can be overcome.

Both parties recognize that for far too long, “America has had a permitting system filled with delays, expenses, red tape, uncertainty,’' she said. “Too long, too expensive. And we’ve seen projects that should be finished more quickly (take) decades” to complete.

The Senate bill would limit legal challenges under the National Environmental Policy Act, a bedrock environmental law that requires federal agencies to consider a project’s possible environmental impacts before it is approved. The law has increasingly been blamed for stalling projects of all types.

Challenges under the National Historic Preservation Act also would be restricted. The law protects Native American cultural treasures and other important artifacts.

The bill would ease siting of interstate transmission lines and strengthen the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s authority to review major projects at the same time as state reviews, helping needed projects move through the overall permitting process more quickly.

The bill also would require data centers to pay for all associated transmission costs, preventing costs from being passed on to families or businesses.

___

Associated Press writer Jennifer McDermott contributed from Providence, R.I.

text:
For years, automotive analysts have been predicting that electric vehicles would become cheaper than their gas-powered equivalents. They figured it would happen sometime in the latter half of the 2020s. BloombergNEF, for example, expected it to happen in 2026.

They weren’t far off.

EV prices have dropped significantly in the last few years, but it has been hard to compare prices with fossil fuel vehicles because not every EV has a like-for-like gas-powered model.

BMW has given us one. The 2027 BMW 3 Series comes in both gas and electric versions, and the EV is $4,400 cheaper.

The gas-powered M350 xDrive will set you back $65,900, while the electric i3 50 xDrive will cost $61,500; neither price includes destination charges. Both are similarly powerful, similarly styled, and aimed at similar pocketbooks. The difference is the EV is 6.7% cheaper.

Pedants will point out there’s a significantly cheaper gas-powered 3 Series trim, though it has no electric equivalent yet. The 2027 BMW 330 is priced at $49,900, and its upgraded xDrive trim costs $51,900.

The two comparable vehicles are built on different platforms, with the EV i3 benefiting from BMW’s newest chassis and technology. The gas-powered 3 Series makes do with an overhauled version of an existing platform.

For most people, the biggest difference will be the charging or refueling experience, but even there they’re more similar than some might expect.

The range of the new gas 3 Series is likely similar to previous models, or about 450 miles per tank in all-wheel-drive guise. The electric i3 will travel 468 miles on a full charge, and BMW says the vehicle’s fast charging is speedy enough to replenish 208 miles of range in 10 minutes. The difference might be noticeable to extreme road warriors, but for most drivers, it’ll be academic.

text:
FedEx has ordered 2,000 all-electric trucks from Harbinger in a deal valued at more than $300 million, the medium-duty manufacturer announced. Delivery is planned by the end of 2027, with the vehicles deployed across North America.

The order is among the largest single commitments to medium-duty electric trucks announced to date, and it comes from a fleet that has already run Harbinger vehicles in service. The order expands on a previously successful deployment of Harbinger vehicles within FedEx operations and follows FedEx’s co-lead investment in Harbinger’s $160 million Series C equity raise.

“FedEx is demonstrating that the business case for incorporating electric vehicles into real-world fleet operations at scale makes sense,” said John Harris, co-founder and CEO of Harbinger.

The OEM estimates the trucks will reduce fuel costs by an average of $20,000 per vehicle per year against conventional equivalents, roughly $40 million annually across the full fleet and approximately $800 million over a 20-year service life. It also projects the deployment will avoid an estimated 1.7 million tons of carbon dioxide emissions over the vehicles’ operating lives.

FedEx framed the order the same way, as an operational and financial decision that also advances an emissions target rather than one made in spite of cost.

“Expanding our deployment of Harbinger vehicles gives us an opportunity to continue making progress toward our fleet electrification goals while reducing fuel and operating costs,” said Paul Melander, senior vice president of safety and transportation at FedEx.

On the product side, Harbinger’s HC Series Cab carries a 26,000-pound gross vehicle weight rating and a 42-foot turning diameter, and the company lists up to 210 miles of range for its electric models. Harbinger engineers its vehicles for a 20-year service life, which is the assumption underneath both the $800 million fuel savings figure and the emissions estimate.

The turning diameter is not a throwaway specification in this application. Pickup and delivery routes put a medium-duty truck into residential streets, alleys and loading zones repeatedly through a shift, and maneuverability at that weight rating is closer to a daily productivity factor than a spec sheet line.

text:
MLB's special-event games, one of the most beloved parts of the league's operations, are hitting an unusual level of turbulence with a potential plan to play at Grand Teton National Park in Wyoming.

League sources said MLB has approached the Trump Administration about the viability of staging a game at a national park, with Grand Teton among the sites discussed. No final decisions have been made, nor have any permits been granted by the National Park Service, and several other unrelated ideas are also under consideration.

Advertisement

Before any formal steps are taken, though, the mere idea of building a temporary ballpark within a national park prompted pushback from a variety of political and business leaders and environmental groups.

"Americans want to see protections for our national parks and public lands strengthened. Bulldozing these lands for a baseball stadium does the opposite, destroying the magnificent landscapes that millions of people come to experience," said Sierra Club Wyoming chapter director Chris Kassar. "It is irresponsible and shortsighted. We can't pretend that a baseball stadium in Grand Teton is in the best interest of Wyomingites."

Seeking the Next Big Thing

MLB's exploration of playing in a national park marks an effort to find the next iteration of its domestic special-event games, which have become key tentpoles within the schedule each year.

Advertisement

Over the past decade, the league has staged three games at the Field of Dreams movie site in Iowa, with a fourth scheduled for 2027, and has also played at Bristol Motor Speedway in Tennessee, Rickwood Field in Alabama, and Fort Bragg in North Carolina. Since 2017, MLB has also played annually in Williamsport, Pennsylvania, in conjunction with the Little League World Series.

Those games have garnered widespread appeal among fans and players, and several milestones have been set, including an MLB single-game attendance record last year in Bristol. The biggest complaint, if any, is that MLB doesn't do more of these special-event games within its 2,430-game regular season.

"I definitely would like to have this be for three days instead of one day," said Phillies star Bryce Harper before this year's Field of Dreams game against the Twins. "I wish it was three days instead of coming in here so quick. It'd be nice to be able to settle down, get the family out there."

The national park consideration, however, has created a rather different vibe.

Advertisement

"Even temporary infrastructure can create lasting impacts through habitat fragmentation, noise and light disturbances, increased human presence in wildlife areas, and strain on park resources," read a joint letter to U.S. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum from leaders of Jackson, Wyoming, the Teton County Commissioners, and the Jackson Hole Chamber of Commerce. "The proposal also risks setting a precedent that major commercial entertainment should occur within protected boundaries."

The White House, meanwhile, said the initial inquiries about the national parks were driven by the league and that it wasn't an "Administration priority."

As the 2027 MLB schedule is now set, any special-event decisions for 2028 and beyond will likely wait until after the league and MLB Players Association grapple with a difficult collective bargaining situation.

“We haven’t landed the plane on mass production of the UEV yet,” Farley said when referring to the platform at the recent Automotive News Congress event in Detroit. “It’s going to be a heck of an effort to launch this at scale, at cost, on time.”

Farley said that Ford is looking at multiple ways to save money on production of the electric truck, which is expected to start at around $30,000. Reaching that price target isn’t going to be easy, especially as the automaker tries to keep the Fathom affordable without making it feel too stripped down.

The Fathom is expected to play an important role in Ford’s push to offer more affordable electric vehicles. Although many electric pickups currently available are expensive and designed to compete with larger trucks (save the coming new $26,400 Slate truck), the Fathom is expected to focus more on value and practicality. That could make it appealing to buyers who want an EV but don’t need the size, power, or price tag of a full-size electric pickup. The vehicle is set to be built at Ford’s Louisville plant, which is currently undergoing a $2 billion retooling.

In a previous interview, Alan Clarke, Ford’s vice president of advanced development projects, told GreenCars that the automaker was working with new suppliers it hadn’t used before. Ford also had to better understand what customers actually wanted in the vehicle, including which features should be included and which could be cut to help keep costs under control.

In short, it’s all easier said than done. Every feature adds cost, weight, and complexity, while removing too much equipment could make the Fathom less competitive against other affordable EVs. Ford will need to find the right balance if it wants to hit the $30,000 price target while still offering a useful and appealing truck.

Multiple Fathom prototypes have been spotted testing in different parts of the country, but Ford has remained tight-lipped about what the truck will offer. Farley didn’t say how far production could be pushed back. Ford had planned to open orders in early 2027 to roughly coincide with the start of production, but that timing could now be in question.

September 30, 2026 (Boston, MA) – Senate lawmakers on Thursday released the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026. Conservation Law Foundation (CLF) released the following statement in response:

“While Conservation Law Foundation has rallied for and secured sensible permitting reforms to expedite the deployment of clean energy infrastructure and other priority projects, the ‘Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026’ (as dubbed by its sponsors) emerged from a backroom negotiation among four Senators, two of them ardent supporters of President’s Trump’s obsessive obstruction of clean energy projects – projects that have demonstrably been the lynchpin to energy affordability in New England,” said CLF President Brad Campbell.

“The more than 400-page bill appears to adopt a fossil fuel industry wish-list, with passage slated before Christmas, sacrificing numerous protections for communities and the environment to achieve outcomes wholly dependent on President Trump’s highly qualified, pre-election assurances that his administration will act in good faith and allow clean energy projects to move forward. Given that Trump has consistently derided and unlawfully obstructed such projects since returning to office, any deal premised on a promise New Englanders know Trump will break has to be considered delusional.

“Striking this deal in the waning days of this Congress, in a pact and on a schedule that preclude public input or amendment, before midterm elections that can only improve the prospects for a more balanced approach, is indefensible.”

CLF experts are available for further comment.

text:
State leaders are providing more insight into the possibility of Oklahoma becoming home to a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus.

The campus would be a research park, an advanced manufacturing center and a technology campus.

"Huge potential, once in a generation potential for the state," said Jeff Starling, Oklahoma Secretary of Energy and Environment.

Earlier this year the U.S. Department of Energy opened a competition for a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus.

The department received 28 applications, and Oklahoma was named a finalist in late July.

"Right now the down select is it will happen by the end of this year for the states and then you know we'll have to work with them on what sites that we're putting forward in Oklahoma actually work with the solutions that they're wanting too. It may be more than one at the end of the day," Starling said.

The campus would consist of three nodes: reactor deployment and isotope production, enrichment through recycling and used nuclear fuel management.

Starling says communities in the state have come forward expressing interest in hosting the campus.

"We started by having the communities in Oklahoma City where we briefed them with Department of Energy officials, Senior Department of Energy officials about a month ago," he said. "We then got into the communities that have identified interest or self-selected. We're never telling them what to do. They've self-selected as wanting to host this campus."

Data center projects have sparked controversy across the state, but Starling says this project is different.

"Data centers are a completely different deal," Starling said. "Data centers come and they add maybe a handful of jobs. This is up to 25,000 jobs across the state. Huge economic input. And this isn't a drain on resources."

Starling said communities that live closest to nuclear are the ones that support it the most.

"We find as people learn more about this campus, the more comfortable they are with the aspects of it," Starling said. "And the economic opportunities that come not only for their kids and grandkids, but their great-grandkids and for future generations of Oklahoma students, our university research programs, the career techs and skilled tradesmen that are needed to operate these facilities."

Oklahoma is one of six states the U.S. Department of Energy is choosing from. The other finalists are West Virginia, Utah, Tennessee, Louisiana and Idaho.

Three states are anticipated to be selected by the end of the year.

John Hudson, chief external affairs officer for Entergy said in the news release that the technology is intended to help provide more reliable and affordable electricity to customers, by "reducing congestion, improving system readiness for large loads and potentially avoiding capital costs for other transmission upgrades."

He said with the federal funding, Entergy will be able to deploy advanced line rating technology across more than 1,000 miles of transmission lines across the three states, which will help boost the amount of power the utility can move through its existing infrastructure.

This is another example of Entergy doing all we can to modernize the electric grid while reducing the financial impacts of these large projects on our customers and communities," Hudson said.

Through the Energy Department's SPARK program, Entergy and its electric companies in Arkansas, Louisiana and Mississippi will implement "dynamic line rating technology, targeted geographic surveys, substation and terminal upgrades across 1,125 miles of existing transmission lines."

According to the news release, the upgrades will help the company more effectively manage energy infrastructure in areas experiencing load growth driven by new industrial development, manufacturing and data center expansion.

The four-year project also establishes a scalable, repeatable model for deploying advanced transmission technologies across multiple operating companies and as constraint shifts over time, Entergy will be able to redeploy dynamic line rating sensors to new corridors.

The project is designed to unlock at least 25% increase in transfer capability on selected transmission corridors, and early modeling has shown the potential for 29% to 61% increase in the project area.

"By expanding the capability of existing transmission corridors, Entergy will be better positioned to support new and expanding industries across the region, helping communities attract investment and sustain long-term economic growth," the news release said.

The Energy Department will spend almost $2 billion on the SPARK program to try and squeeze more electricity out of the nation's electric grid.

The money will go toward 31 projects across 26 states that are expected to produce more than 23 gigawatts of additional electricity capacity -- enough to power 16 million homes, The Associated Press reported. The projects will use new technologies such as sensors to measure real-time weather conditions to ensure safe transmission or direct power away from congested paths, the department said.

Mercedes-Benz has strengthened its decade-long partnership with ProLogium to gain priority access to its fourth-generation solid-state battery cells, marking a significant advancement in EV technology.

Solid-state batteries offer higher energy density, faster charging, and increased safety compared to traditional lithium-ion cells. Mercedes-Benz is partnering with ProLogium to test these Gen4 lithium ceramic batteries, aiming to integrate the technology into its next-generation electric vehicles within the coming year.

“At Mercedes-Benz, we are committed to shaping the future of electric mobility,” said Jörg Burzer, Board of Management member. “Our partnership with ProLogium helps us advance next-generation battery technology. By combining ProLogium’s solid-state expertise with our development capabilities, we are reaching a milestone in evolving our future electric vehicle fleet.”

ProLogium currently operates a significant battery manufacturing facility in Taiwan and is planning a new site in Dunkirk, France, with a projected capacity of up to 44 GWh. This facility is expected to facilitate the supply of cells to European customers, including Mercedes-Benz.

Beyond its collaboration with ProLogium, Mercedes-Benz is actively diversifying its solid-state battery initiatives by testing lithium-metal battery cells from the American firm Factorial Energy.

In a notable development last year, a Mercedes-Benz EQS equipped with a Factorial solid-state battery pack successfully achieved a range of 748.8 miles (1,205 km) on a single charge. The test concluded with approximately 85 miles (137 km) of estimated range remaining, demonstrating the significant potential of this technology.

description:
That source is nuclear energy.
Many fear nuclear energy, repelled by concerns over toxic radioactive waste or world-ending meltdowns and explosions.
For context, nuclear energy is created in reactors within nuclear power plants through the process of nuclear fission; it uses atomic particles of the chemical element uranium, one of the heaviest naturally occurring elements on earth.
Returning to the paranoia people have surrounding nuclear energy as a whole, it certainly is understandable.
Nuclear energy disasters like Chernobyl and Fukushima scare many away from accepting nuclear energy, viewing it as playing with fire.
text:
Coming off of the latest brutally hot summer, a topic fresh in the minds of many, including myself, is climate change. The overall reaction to the approaching climate apocalypse from the public and powers at large has been shocking, as far as one would expect apocalypse reactions to go.

This is due to the fundamental challenge at the heart of responding to climate change — to lower emissions in our current oil- and gas-powered global economy, it would require very powerful people who have made a lot of money through the petroleum industry to independently give up their fortunes and levers of global control and work towards greener energy for the greater good. Something they clearly do not want to do in our increasingly data-center filled planet of today. It would also require world leaders to accept that less powerful energy sources should be made to phase out fossil fuels, which yield higher amounts of energy and power than options such as solar or wind power.

However, within the clean energy sector, there does exist a power source that provides vastly higher amounts of energy per unit than fossil fuels do all while keeping emissions just as low as other green alternatives. That source is nuclear energy. Many fear nuclear energy, repelled by concerns over toxic radioactive waste or world-ending meltdowns and explosions. However, these are threats that can be highly mitigated; given the real threat at hand, which is climate change, I think it is time to revisit solutions that some may deem too radical.

For context, nuclear energy is created in reactors within nuclear power plants through the process of nuclear fission; it uses atomic particles of the chemical element uranium, one of the heaviest naturally occurring elements on earth. These atoms are bombarded by extremely high-speed neutrons, which cause them to break down and split into new, smaller elements. (Similar to what occurs in a nuclear bomb, but without the massive explosion!) This releases a massive amount of energy, which is absorbed into a very large quantity of water, which rapidly heats and creates lots of steam. This chain reaction causes turbines within the powerplant to spin extremely quickly, this step being what actually generates electricity and energy. So when you look at a nuclear power plant and see massive plumes of white smoke, it is simply steam; not radioactive waste or polluting carbon. It’s clean; it’s just water!

In terms of energy creation, this process is actually superior in efficiency to fossil fuels. The reason that oil is a more powerful source of energy than green alternatives like wind or solar is that it has a much higher energy density. This means that burning, say, one kilogram of oil is equivalent to using a massive amount of something like solar energy, which is why it is so coveted by any and all institutions that want to build and create. However, by these same metrics, nuclear’s efficiency blows fossil fuels out of the water. To compare it to coal, utilizing just one gram of uranium within a nuclear reactor is equivalent to over 1.5 tons of coal. Clean energy sources like spring power and gas illustrate that the nuclear fission process creates millions times the energy of oil and gas per unit of mass. All of this gain would come at no environmental detriment; it would actually massively help the global emissions problem, with a vast majority of the energy created today coming from fossil fuels.

Returning to the paranoia people have surrounding nuclear energy as a whole, it certainly is understandable. Nuclear energy disasters like Chernobyl and Fukushima scare many away from accepting nuclear energy, viewing it as playing with fire. To that, I would say two things. Firstly, modern solutions to problems like these do exist. Modern-day radiation scientists have tested solutions to problems of the past, such as deep underground containers where nuclear waste can be stored, theoretically able to hold waste for thousands of years into the future without toxic leakage.

Secondly, I would consider the devastating effects that a fossil fuel-based global energy system has already wreaked on our planet. We are currently facing, potentially within our own lifetimes, the global catastrophic concerns that many fear nuclear energy might bring. Earth is currently facing drastic heatwaves, wildfires and ecosystem disruptions at an unprecedented rate. Climate refugees have already begun to flee these disasters en masse and it will only continue and intensify for years to come without drastic action. There’s a reason so many scientists think the world could be made uninhabitable and that we have very little time to fix it.

While for some this may border on conspiracy, many believe oil interests to be at the heart of international conflicts that have led to the devastation of millions of lives. Examples such as the 2003 Iraq War, America’s bombing of Libya in 2011 and Trump’s recent attack on Venezuela all share a common denominator of oil companies profiting and gaining access to higher supplies of petroleum. The owners of these oil companies, like Shell, ExxonMobil and Chevron, directly lobby our politicians and encourage more war and more death on behalf of fossil fuel acquisition. Who is to say the children who were killed in the U.S. invasion on Iraq are not equal victims of oil policy to someone killed due to droughts or floods?

Uranium, on the other hand, is much more globally common than oil and fossil fuels, being found underground in many, many regions of the world, where oil’s relative rarity makes it very valuable and powerful in the instances where it is discovered. This means that further global reliance on uranium and not fossil fuels could lead to more independence and self-sufficiency for many places in the world that are victims of the manipulative oil market and remain subservient to the U.S. dollar, which oil is globally priced in. This is especially true, since as mentioned prior, a mere handful of uranium could be enough to power huge growth and development. Not only could nuclear energy be used to drastically lower emissions in terms of climate change, but it could also level the playing field in a world that is so unequal in its current state. Unless you have a vested interest in the status quo, which those keeping oil as our primary energy source do, rethinking paranoia surrounding nuclear power before it’s too late would be very wise.

text:
Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin said the Trump administration is right on schedule to approve by year’s end changes needed to permanently eliminate mandatory safety and emission inspections for cars and trucks in New Hampshire.

At a roundtable at the New Hampshire Institute of Politics, Zeldin, a former four-term congressman, said he would not prejudge the agency's final rulemaking.

But Zeldin said he agreed with Republican legislative leaders that eliminating emissions inspections is broadly popular among New Hampshire residents.

“The commitment was to complete this before the end of this year. We are still on track to get this done,” Zeldin said, poking fun at Region 1 Administrator Mark Sanborn, a Laconia resident. “They might want to relocate you to Massachusetts if you don’t get this done.”

The comment period ended last Friday for the EPA staff’s recommendation to allow New Hampshire to leave the Ozone Transport Region (OTR) and to change its Clean Air Act compliance plan to permanently get rid of inspections.

Patrick Bird, deputy air division director with EPA Region 1, said his team is evaluating more than 400 pages of comments from individuals, environmental and business groups along with the vendor the state abruptly fired when it stopped the emissions program earlier this winter.

“We are working through these facts. Any response to the comments will be contained in the final action regarding this matter,” Bird said.

House Majority Leader Jason Osborne, R-Auburn, said there’s been no action the Republican-led Legislature has taken in the past debate that has been more popular.

“Inflation has escalated, we have to find those things that can be fixed,” Osborne began. “There is not a lot we can do in a tiny state with a global economy that can make a difference in peoples’ wallets and pocketbooks. This is one of those things.”

Year after year, interest groups defending these emissions hired lobbyists to kill changes to reduce the scope of these inspections, Osborne said.

“We decided this was the way to do it once and for all. I can’t thank you enough and our own DES (Department of Environmental Services) for working to get this done,” Osborne told Zeldin.

Clean Air Act led to mandatory emissions tests

The state adopted mandatory inspections after parts of the state’s air quality was found to have excessive levels of ozone. The state’s compliance with the federal Clean Air Act called for New Hampshire to join the OTR.

Environmental Services Commissioner Bob Scott said the EPA has always been a helpful partner to make the environmental mandates as cost effective for New Hampshire consumers as they could be.

“The Clean Air Act has an off ramp for a reason. This is a success story,” Scott said, pointing to improving air quality standards in recent years.

House Deputy Majority Leader Joe Sweeney, R-Salem, said federal environmental laws were adopted in the 1960s and 1970s with “good intentions,” but improving technology have rendered them less relevant and more onerous.

“We are constantly looking to make sure those regulations are not a barrier to economic growth in New Hampshire,” Sweeney said. “Our laws in this state were not in reality to the improving shape of the vehicles that were on the road.”

A representative with Gordon-Darby Holdings, the inspections vendor, said New Hampshire threatens to put citizens at risk by eliminating these tests permanently.

“New Hampshire may meet all federal air quality standards on a statewide level, but attainment data reflects regional averages rather than the specific street-level air quality an individual breathes every day,” Gordon-Darby said in its statement.

“In more densely populated areas, localized factors like heavy traffic, idling vehicles, and concentrated commercial activity can create micro-scale environments where pollution levels are higher than the regional average. For individuals like Marilyn (Jonas of Wilton), living with chronic respiratory conditions such as asthma, even subtle changes in air quality or the removal of localized control strategies can have a noticeable, real-world impact on their health.”

Environmental opponents to the changes pointed to the American Lung Association’s 27th annual “State of the Air” report.

"The Boston–Worcester–Providence, MA–RI–NH metro area (which includes five of the state’s ten counties, and 79% of the state’s population) continues to struggle with unhealthy air quality, earning failing grades for both ozone smog and short-term particle pollution, despite showing improvement in year-round particle pollution levels,” the report said.

Zeldin said the Clean Air Act was not adopted to impose restrictions to deal with climate change, and that would be a further act for Congress to make.

“My message to Congress is if you want us to regulate the heck out of greenhouse emission standards then change the law and we will follow that law,” Zeldin added.

title: Senate reaches bipartisan deal on permitting bill to speed approvals of new energy projects
description:
But the bill represents a rare instance of bipartisanship over the country's energy policy as lawmakers from both parties agree on the need to build new energy projects of all types.
He and Heinrich, the top energy Democrat, have decried what they call Trump's "reckless and vindictive assault on wind energy" that includes repeated actions to block large-scale wind projects under construction off the East Coast.
The administration suspended five offshore wind projects in December, citing unspecified national security concerns.
A federal judge also struck down Trump's executive order blocking wind energy projects early in his second term.
Trump recently offered to ease his administration's holdup on renewable energy projects, in part to entice Democrats to agree to a permitting deal.
text:
Republican Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia, chair of the Environment and Public Works Committee, called the bill "a major step toward making it faster and more efficient and easier to build infrastructure projects" of all types while maintaining important environmental protections.

Vote on the bill won't happen until after the midterms

"The American people sent us here to do big things. This is a big thing. It's monumental and it's legacy-setting," Capito said at a news conference at the Capitol where she was joined by Republican Sen. Mike Lee of Utah and Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island. The four senators lead the chamber's energy and environment panels.

Heinrich said the bill "will mean more energy on the grid, more good-paying jobs, and lower electricity costs for families and businesses. And as data centers drive demand for more power, it will ensure they pay their fair share of the grid upgrades they require – not leave that bill to American families."

A vote on the bill won't happen until after the midterm elections — reflecting the fraught political reality as elections loom that could change partisan control of both chambers. But the bill represents a rare instance of bipartisanship over the country's energy policy as lawmakers from both parties agree on the need to build new energy projects of all types.

Lee, who chairs the energy committee, said he is confident the bill will be approved in a lame-duck session in November, noting its bipartisan support and encouragement from business and environmental groups.

READ MORE: Energy Department will spend nearly $2 billion to squeeze more electricity from the nation's aging power grid

Whitehouse, the top Democrat on the environment panel, also was hopeful but said Democrats were still seeking clarity on how the bill will prevent President Donald Trump's administration from blocking wind and solar projects.

He and Heinrich, the top energy Democrat, have decried what they call Trump's "reckless and vindictive assault on wind energy" that includes repeated actions to block large-scale wind projects under construction off the East Coast. The administration suspended five offshore wind projects in December, citing unspecified national security concerns.

The projects later moved forward after federal judges intervened. A federal judge also struck down Trump's executive order blocking wind energy projects early in his second term.

Brad Campbell, president of the Conservation Law Foundation, an environmental advocacy group, panned the deal, saying it "appears to adopt a fossil fuel industry wish-list." He said the bill could roll back clean water and endangered species protections, limit judicial review and curtail the power of the Environmental Protection Agency and states to consider impacts of energy projects.

"Striking this deal in the waning days of this Congress, in a pact and on a schedule that preclude public input or amendment, before midterm elections that can only improve the prospects for a more balanced approach, is indefensible," Campbell said in a statement.

In a statement, the White House said the bill would "deliver transformative policies to lower Americans' energy and housing costs, drive new construction and investment in American infrastructure, and create American jobs."

Trump's wind opposition played a role in delaying a deal

Trump's opposition to wind power has been a consistent stumbling block to a deal on permitting reform, which Democrats say can only go forward if the administration agrees to allow previously approved projects to move forward.

Trump recently offered to ease his administration's holdup on renewable energy projects, in part to entice Democrats to agree to a permitting deal.

Whitehouse called the proposal reasonable but said the overall issue remains "unresolved."

Capito was confident such obstacles can be overcome.

WATCH: Why the Trump administration is paying billions to abandon wind farms

Both parties recognize that for far too long, "America has had a permitting system filled with delays, expenses, red tape, uncertainty,'' she said. "Too long, too expensive. And we've seen projects that should be finished more quickly (take) decades" to complete.

The Senate bill would limit legal challenges under the National Environmental Policy Act, a bedrock environmental law that requires federal agencies to consider a project's possible environmental impacts before it is approved. The law has increasingly been blamed for stalling projects of all types.

Challenges under the National Historic Preservation Act also would be restricted. The law protects Native American cultural treasures and other important artifacts.

The bill would ease siting of interstate transmission lines and strengthen the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission's authority to review major projects at the same time as state reviews, helping needed projects move through the overall permitting process more quickly.

The bill also would require data centers to pay for all associated transmission costs, preventing costs from being passed on to families or businesses.

Associated Press writer Jennifer McDermott contributed from Providence, R.I.

authors: MATTHEW DALY Associated Press, ABC News

text:
WASHINGTON -- Senators from both parties said Wednesday they have reached a bipartisan deal on legislation aimed at speeding up permitting reviews for new energy and infrastructure projects that now face yearslong delays as lawmakers seek to meet growing demand for electricity and other forms of energy.

The bill, proponents argue, would cut down the arduous timeline for getting big energy projects off the ground at a time when demand is rising because of mushrooming data centers for AI. The bill would ensure data centers are forced to pay for the increased electricity they use and would mark a significant change to a landmark environmental law that critics say slows down the process of building energy products.

Republican Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia, chair of the Environment and Public Works Committee, called the bill “a major step toward making it faster and more efficient and easier to build infrastructure projects” of all types while maintaining important environmental protections.

“The American people sent us here to do big things. This is a big thing. It’s monumental and it’s legacy-setting,” Capito said at a news conference at the Capitol where she was joined by Republican Sen. Mike Lee of Utah and Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island. The four senators lead the chamber's energy and environment panels.

Heinrich said the bill “will mean more energy on the grid, more good-paying jobs, and lower electricity costs for families and businesses. And as data centers drive demand for more power, it will ensure they pay their fair share of the grid upgrades they require – not leave that bill to American families."

A vote on the bill won’t happen until after the midterm elections — reflecting the fraught political reality as elections loom that could change partisan control of both chambers. But the bill represents a rare instance of bipartisanship over the country’s energy policy as lawmakers from both parties agree on the need to build new energy projects of all types.

Lee, who chairs the energy committee, said he is confident the bill will be approved in a lame-duck session in November, noting its bipartisan support and encouragement from business and environmental groups.

Whitehouse, the top Democrat on the environment panel, also was hopeful but said Democrats were still seeking clarity on how the bill will prevent President Donald Trump's administration from blocking wind and solar projects.

He and Heinrich, the top energy Democrat, have decried what they call Trump's “reckless and vindictive assault on wind energy” that includes repeated actions to block large-scale wind projects under construction off the East Coast. The administration suspended five offshore wind projects in December, citing unspecified national security concerns.

The projects later moved forward after federal judges intervened. A federal judge also struck down Trump’s executive order blocking wind energy projects early in his second term.

Brad Campbell, president of the Conservation Law Foundation, an environmental advocacy group, panned the deal, saying it “appears to adopt a fossil fuel industry wish-list.” He said the bill could roll back clean water and endangered species protections, limit judicial review and curtail the power of the Environmental Protection Agency and states to consider impacts of energy projects.

“Striking this deal in the waning days of this Congress, in a pact and on a schedule that preclude public input or amendment, before midterm elections that can only improve the prospects for a more balanced approach, is indefensible,” Campbell said in a statement.

In a statement, the White House said the bill would “deliver transformative policies to lower Americans’ energy and housing costs, drive new construction and investment in American infrastructure, and create American jobs.”

Trump's opposition to wind power has been a consistent stumbling block to a deal on permitting reform, which Democrats say can only go forward if the administration agrees to allow previously approved projects to move forward.

Trump recently offered to ease his administration’s holdup on renewable energy projects, in part to entice Democrats to agree to a permitting deal.

Whitehouse called the proposal reasonable but said the overall issue remains “unresolved.”

Capito was confident such obstacles can be overcome.

Both parties recognize that for far too long, “America has had a permitting system filled with delays, expenses, red tape, uncertainty,'' she said. "Too long, too expensive. And we’ve seen projects that should be finished more quickly (take) decades” to complete.

The Senate bill would limit legal challenges under the National Environmental Policy Act, a bedrock environmental law that requires federal agencies to consider a project’s possible environmental impacts before it is approved. The law has increasingly been blamed for stalling projects of all types.

Challenges under the National Historic Preservation Act also would be restricted. The law protects Native American cultural treasures and other important artifacts.

The bill would ease siting of interstate transmission lines and strengthen the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s authority to review major projects at the same time as state reviews, helping needed projects move through the overall permitting process more quickly.

The bill also would require data centers to pay for all associated transmission costs, preventing costs from being passed on to families or businesses.

___

Associated Press writer Jennifer McDermott contributed from Providence, R.I.

text:
Ionna — one of the newest EV fast-charging networks in the US — has had a heck of a growth spurt during its first year of operation. This week, it announced that it now has more than 180 live sites nationwide, more than doubling its footprint since the start of 2026. According to the company’s reckoning, that makes Ionna “the largest 400-kilowatt fast charging network in the US,” a very specific claim worth examining.

I spoke with Ionna CEO Seth Cutler about the network’s rapid expansion, the new features rolling out and what Ionna is doing to make DC fast charging even more affordable for EV drivers.

Ionna was founded in July 2023 as a joint venture among seven major automakers: BMW, General Motors, Honda, Hyundai, Kia, Mercedes-Benz and Stellantis. Later, in July 2024, Toyota joined the venture as an investor, bringing the total to eight companies on the board. The fledgling network opened its first “Rechargery” — the brand’s name for its brightly colored, retro-styled fast charging stations — in Apex, North Carolina, in December 2024.

Less than two years later, Ionna’s network now includes more than 180 stations with over 1,500 charging ports across 30 states.

Largest 400 kW network*

From that first station in Apex, every Ionna Rechargery site has featured plugs for both the Combined Charging System and the North American Charging Standard, reducing the need to fiddle with adapters. The Rechargeries are also noteworthy for their standardization of high-powered 400-kW charging stalls. That’s faster than the average EV on sale in the US can accept, so drivers are less likely to find their charging sessions throttled when plugging in.

“We’ve built out a network for the future at 400 kilowatts,” Cutler told me during a video call. “New vehicles are coming with much higher native charging speeds — the BMW iX3 is a good example, as well as some Lexus and Toyota products coming to market soon. This network is built for them. Right now, we’re the largest 400 kW network and expect to continue to be for some time.”

That “largest 400 kW network” boast is an interesting one. Ionna is far from the largest DC fast charging network in the US. Tesla’s Supercharger network has had a 12-year head start and comprises over 3,000 locations — about half of all DC fast-charging ports in the country — across all 50 states. Second and third places go to EVgo and Electrify America, with about 1,200 and 1,000 sites, respectively.

However, those networks typically top out at around 325-350 kW, with some older stalls as low as 50-150 kW. That’s good enough for most of today’s EVs, but Ionna’s higher-powered bet may matter more down the road. Plus, it’s a very specific “largest” trophy for the brand to claim.

No app, no problem

During my recent EV road trip, I decided to stop by one of Ionna’s new Rechargeries in Sacramento, California. Before setting out, I tried to grab the requisite app and set up my account — as you would with every other EV charging network — and was amused to find that Ionna doesn’t have a proprietary app. There’s a web portal where you can search for stations, but the entire payment process takes place at the plug. Cutler says this decision was all about removing friction.

“When we first started the company, we asked, ‘What’s the first thing you need?’ and everyone put their hands up and said, ‘We need a charging app,’” Cutler recalled. “The problem we had was quantifying the why. Why do you need an app? What we’ve found is that the No. 1 reason people ask about an app is to know where our chargers are, but no one’s asking for an app because they want to pay better or pay more easily. We really want to remove friction, not add friction to the ecosystem.”

Instead, Ionna chose to work on integrating with 19 partner platforms, including recently announced collaborations with Presto, ChargeHub and EV Connect. For payments, the network focused on Plug & Charge support and Tap to Pay. Plug & Charge is a payment tech that lets drivers start charging and automatically pay simply by plugging their car into a compatible station. Ionna announced that it’s enabling compatibility with Volvo Cars, with Toyota and Lexus to follow in October. That will bring the total to nine automakers that can Plug & Charge, including Rivian, which is not on the Ionna board.

The new Driver Dashboard

Drivers also have the option to simply tap a credit card at the stall. (As a reviewer who is often charging fleet vehicles, this is my preferred method, and the Rechargeries I’ve visited are about as close to a gas station payment experience as I’ve had with an EV.)

Cutler told me that most drivers who use Ionna stations use their automakers’ apps to monitor their charging session from afar, but for drivers who don’t want to do even that, it has introduced a new Driver’s Dashboard which can be accessed via a QR code displayed on the charger. The code opens a web portal that tracks the current session, with no download, account or password required.

“So you can walk away and at least see what state of charge your vehicle is in and when your car will be done, or how much power you’re pulling,” Cutler said.

Making charging more affordable

Ionna also announced on Wednesday that Hyundai and Mercedes-Benz will soon offer drivers discounted energy rates (around 10% off) through their apps when charging at an Ionna Rechargery via Plug & Charge. The brands join BMW (20%) and GM (10%) in offering their own discounts, with more automakers potentially to come.

Ionna’s current maximum base rate of 39 cents per kWh (plus applicable taxes) across its entire network is already a pretty good deal compared to competitors charging up to 65 cents per kWh at peak. For context, on my recent EV road trip, a 10-80% charge for a Chevy Equinox EV cost $43.27 at a Tesla Supercharger, while my next 20-80% charge at a Rechargery was just $16.47 without the GM discount.

“We believe at Ionna that our job is to build out a quality-at-scale charging network to unlock adoption of EVs,” Cutler said. “And part of that has to be the affordability of charging, because if it’s too expensive, it totally changes the equation of total cost of ownership of owning an EV versus an internal combustion engine.”

I asked Cutler what more Ionna could be doing for urban drivers who often rely exclusively on public charging — those stuck paying what experts call the “Renters’ Penalty,” spending up to six times more for charging than homeowners who can charge cheaply at home.

“We are piloting time-of-use rates in a couple of locations, and we’re having conversations about expanding that more broadly next year as another tool in our chest,” Cutler said. “We’re finding levers to pull from an affordability standpoint, and we’re not done yet in terms of driving progress there.”

INDIANAPOLIS -- Gov. Mike Braun announced Indiana's renewed statewide energy emergency and the extended suspension of the state’s Gasoline Use Tax and Gasoline Excise Tax through Nov. 4.

“Affordability is my top priority, and my gas tax suspensions have delivered immediate tax relief and some of the cheapest gas in America for Hoosier families. I'm delivering relief for Hoosier farmers by lifting special fuel restrictions to help ease the burden and providing relief from high gas prices to keep more money in Hoosiers’ pockets and make life more affordable," stated Braun.

Braun added he's also suspending the special fuel restrictions for dyed diesel, allowing farmers to use dyed diesel for any farm related activities.

The governor states this is a direct response to concerns raised by the farming community.

Braun's office states the renewal comes after continued disruptions to the global oil supply, including recent Houthi drone attacks in Saudi Arabia that shut down the East-West Pipeline, which accounts for 7 percent of the world’s oil supply.

The governor's office also notes Houthi military advances in Yemen that also threaten oil shipments through the Red Sea, while the ongoing war between Russia and Ukraine continues to disrupt crude oil supplies, leaving Russia’s refining capacity near its lowest level this century.

Valmet, a leading global developer and supplier of process technologies, automation and services for the energy, pulp and paper industries, was selected by Strategic Biofuels to provide biomass power generation and flue gas cleaning technologies for its Louisiana Green Fuels (LGF) project in Caldwell Parish, Louisiana.

text:
Valmet, a leading global developer and supplier of process technologies, automation and services for the energy, pulp and paper industries, was selected by Strategic Biofuels to provide biomass power generation and flue gas cleaning technologies for its Louisiana Green Fuels (LGF) project in Caldwell Parish, Louisiana. The project is designed to integrate carbon-negative power generated from renewable forestry residuals with carbon capture and permanent geologic sequestration to produce deeply carbon-negative electric power.

Under its planned scope of work, Valmet will provide a boiler island featuring a circulating fluidized bed (CFB) boiler and advanced flue gas cleaning systems. The company’s unmatched large-scale proven biomass technologies are designed to support fuel flexibility, operational reliability and environmental performance while helping customers achieve ambitious sustainability objectives.

“Strategic Biofuels has cultivated strong partners for each area of this project to help ensure smooth and successful execution. By combining renewable power generation with carbon capture and sequestration, the project creates meaningful benefits for both the environment and the local community. Valmet’s expertise in biomass-fired boiler technology and flue gas cleaning supports the project’s goals for operational reliability, environmental performance, and long-term efficiency. We look forward to contributing to the project’s continued development,” says Lauri Pehu-Lehtonen, Vice President, Energy and Circularity, Valmet.

The LGF project is designed for more than 300 megawatts of gross generating capacity. At full buildout, the project is expected to annually consume more than 3.5 million tons of sustainably sourced forestry residuals, approximately 400 truckloads of biomass per day. The project’s post-combustion carbon capture and sequestration system is designed to capture and permanently store carbon dioxide in a fully permitted geologic reservoir.

Dive Brief:

Perdue Farms announced earlier this month it’s launching an environmental board of trade which looks to standardize regenerative agriculture standards for things like insetting scope 3 emissions claims, voluntary carbon credits and clean fuel credit certificates. The board also seeks to boost governance and transparency in the sector to help scale agricultural environmental attributes and bring more credibility to such solutions.

The initiative was launched with carbon dioxide removal standard-setter and registry Puro.earth, regenerative agriculture company Arva Intelligence and environment-focused geospatial company Millpoint.

The formation of the board was tied to Puro.earth’s launch of an environmental attributes credits registry, which will initially focus on credits tied to agricultural carbon intensity, according to a Sept. 17 press release. Perdue and Arva are also serving as the first adopters of the nascent registry.

Dive Insight:

The environmental board of trade initiative has been established as a nonprofit 501(c)(6) organization, similar to a business league or trade association, according to the release. Its first priorities will be working to standardize environmental attribute methodologies for scope 3 insetting for agricultural supply chains, certificates necessary for 45Z clean fuel production tax credits or credits rewarded to domestic producers of low-emission transportation and aviation fuels, voluntary carbon credits and credits that certify environmental co-benefit claims.

Currently, it takes the company a long time to close deals that seek to sell carbon credits to its downstream customers, Perdue Farms Director of Sustainability Ben Hildebrand told ESG Dive in an interview. The process requires both parties getting comfortable with a methodology and data sharing expectations, Hildebrand said, but noted that Perdue looks to work with the industry to reach a place where a deal timeline can go from a three-month science review to being completed in two weeks, through the establishment of “a trusted system.”

“Everybody’s asking the farmer for data; if it’s not us, then it’s the next guy, and maybe it’s three different companies that are asking the farmer for data,” Hildebrand said. “So, part of it is [that] there’s just a lot of inefficiency in how we’re getting what we need in order to create value for the farmer off of what they’re doing.”

If the industry grows to trust the registry and the EBOT, it will be possible to reduce the frequency of data requests and remove some unnecessary cost, Hildebrand said.

Puro.earth’s environmental attributes registry will run separately from its carbon dioxide removal registry, with an initial focus on credits tied to farmers’ agricultural carbon intensity scores. Puro said its registry will establish carbon intensity scores of agriculture commodities; link it to a defined production quantity, origin site, production period and geospatial records; and keep records of the buyer.

The environmental attribute certificates registry for agricultural products is coming online around the same time as a few related regulations, frameworks and reporting requirements go into effect. The Science Based Targets initiative has its Forest, Land and Agriculture guidance; the Greenhouse Gas Protocol’s land sector and removal standard goes into effect Jan. 1, 2027; the 45Z clean fuel credit requires carbon intensity data; the European Union’s Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive has a scope 3 emissions reporting requirement.

Puro.earth President Jan-Willem Bode said in the release that the new registry will apply its existing expertise and infrastructure to a new asset class. Bode said EBOT’s adoption of the registry is a “testament to the rigor and trust Puro.earth brings to the market.”

“As crop producers and buyers come under pressure from climate risks and regulatory scrutiny, the new Registry helps them lower their carbon intensity, prove it and be rewarded for it, while building healthier soil and more resilient supply chains,” Bode said.

Scott Raubenstine, vice president of agricultural services at Perdue Agribusiness — a division of Perdue that focuses on agricultural commodities and animal nutrition products — said that the EBOT looks to “spin the flywheel of scaling” and help expand regenerative agriculture practices the company seeks to implement on farms in its own supply chain for decarbonization.

Congress must act to lower energy bills, protect clean air and water, and transition off of fossil fuels, and that means making it faster and easier to build transmission and clean energy.

text:
Washington, DC - Today, Senators Capito, Lee, Heinrich, and Whitehouse introduced the “Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026,” a bill intended to speed the permitting of infrastructure and energy projects.

In reaction, Sierra Club’s Chief Program Officer Holly Bender released the following statement:

“There is no task more urgent than building clean energy and transmission. Congress must act to lower energy bills, protect clean air and water, and transition off of fossil fuels, and that means making it faster and easier to build transmission and clean energy. We are still reviewing this new 400+ page package. But this bill cannot guarantee that more wind and solar projects will actually get built as long as the Trump administration continues to block them at every turn. Meanwhile, the proposed text would create immediate benefits for oil and gas companies during a period of unprecedented growth in oil and gas infrastructure and record-breaking industry profits, while communities stand to lose critical protections for clean air, water, and wildlife. Sierra Club is ready to work with champions in Congress to ensure we can accelerate the deployment of clean energy without undermining key environmental and public health protections for communities and locking us into fossil fuels for generations to come.”
