text:
Justice Gorsuch is wrong about the cure, but delegation has gotten out of hand.

Summary

Congress has given the President very broad national security and emergency powers, which have been abused to pursue ordinary policy goals. Justice Gorsuch is right that we should worry about such broad delegations of power, but he's wrong about the remedy. Congress should put time limits on these presidential actions, and courts should scrutinize them to make sure they have some plausible basis.

Justice Gorsuch has made it a personal crusade to revive the nondelegation doctrine, in part because of concerns about the rising tide of presidential power. As I’ll explain below, the nondelegation doctrine tries to limit the ability of Congress to delegate authority to the executive branch. Strengthening the doctrine is an unworkable solution, but Gorsuch is right that Congress has put far too much trust in the good faith and sound judgment of the President and his subordinates. That’s especially true with respect to national security and emergency powers. Environmental law provides more than enough examples.

The nondelegation doctrine is based on the separation of powers. The idea is that the Constitution gives Congress the power to make laws and the President the power to implement them. If, instead, Congress told the President to make up whatever rules he wants, he would be essentially making law rather than implementing it. The problem is that there’s no real way for a court to decide when Congress has given the President “too much” discretion.

Gorsuch is right that executive discretion has become a real problem. The executive branch under Trump has run amok in its use of emergency power, which is not to say his predecessors were completely restrained either. He’s been President about 10% of the fifty years since the National Emergencies Act was passed but has issued 25% of all national emergencies. On the first day of his second term, he declared a national energy emergency. He claimed that “the United States’ insufficient energy production, transportation, refining, and generation constitutes an unusual and extraordinary threat to our Nation’s economy, national security, and foreign policy.” The emergency was a fiction. The U.S. had plenty of energy. In response, agencies like the Army Corps of Engineers took hundreds of emergency actions, all at the expense of the environment.

Justice Gorsuch was right on point in a speech last week when he decried ““[t]he rise of the emergency. The perpetual emergency. Everything is an emergency.” He added “I just don’t think that’s a recipe for a healthy democracy over the long term.” Absolutely right.

Trump and his subordinates have also been all too willing to find threats to national security. I posted a dozen examples recently. Those dire security threats included restraints on oil drilling to protect whales in the Gulf of Mexico, restrictions on toxics emissions from a half dozen industries, and radar reflections from windmills.

These abuses of power are based on extremely broad delegations. The National Emergencies Act doesn’t attempt to define emergencies. The courts refuse to review emergency declarations, so the President has carte blanche to trigger emergency powers. National security calls to mind foreign soldiers or military threats, but today the definition has become very broad and covers just about anything the President decides is bad for the country.

For example, the Defense Production Act allows the President to run roughshod over the economy to “ensure the vitality of the domestic industrial base.” The theory is that “the security of the United States is dependent on the ability of the domestic industrial base to supply materials and services for the national defense and to prepare for and respond to military conflicts, natural or man-caused disasters, or acts of terrorism within the United States.” When the Trump Administration wanted to restart a small oil pipeline near Santa Barbara despite state law (probably as a poke in the eye for Governor Newsom), they reached for the Defense Production Act. And why not, given the vague standard for invoking powerful legal authority?

In the Trump tariff case, the Court pointed out the threat of executive abuse that is posed by emergency statutes: “The Government reads [an economic emergency law] to give the President power to unilaterally impose unbounded tariffs. On this reading, moreover, the President is unconstrained by the significant procedural limitations in other tariff statutes and free to issue a dizzying array of modifications at will. All it takes to unlock that extraordinary power is a Presidential declaration of emergency, which the Government asserts is unreviewable.” Just so.

Justice Gorsuch’s pet solution, the nondelegation doctrine, was called into use for the first and last times in 1935. (The doctrine first surfaced in a 19th Century Supreme Court decision.) It was never used to strike down a federal law in the 146 years before that, nor in the 91 years after. There’s a good reason for that. It’s impossible to draw a principled line for when a delegation “goes too far.” The question of how tightly to constrain the executive branch’s implementation of law is inherently a policy decision. But that doesn’t mean that we need to ignore the possibility of abuse, which has become all too real.

Congress tried in the 1976 National Emergencies Act to rein in presidential power, but that part of the law turned out to be unconstitutional, leaving the President a completely free hand. An alternative solution adopted by many states is to put a time limit on emergency powers and require legislative action to extent them. That makes complete sense to me. A six month or one year deadline would give Congress plenty of time to consider a problem and act.

That solution would require legislation. In the meantime, I’d suggest that courts should rethink their kneejerk deference to declarations of emergencies or national security threats. There are good reasons to be deferential to these actions. Crises may demand quick responses, and judges may be ill-positioned to determine the need for action. But deference should not mean complete surrender. Courts should still stand ready to demand some plausible explanation for the President’s action.

text:
Electrified Materials (EMCO), the majority-owned recycling subsidiary of American Resources, has signed a binding letter of intent (LOI) to acquire all of the equity in Blackion, a lithium-ion battery lifecycle and critical materials company. The all-stock deal values Blackion at about $13.2 million, based on an agreed $275 million pre-money valuation of EMCO.

Blackion handles feedstock origination, reverse logistics, battery lifecycle management, material recovery, traceability and closed-loop supply chain services, and it has operations and relationships in the US and abroad.

In July 2025, Blackion, EMCO and refiner ReElement Technologies announced an LFP recycling collaboration. Under that collaboration, Blackion would source end-of-life battery material and EMCO would disassemble and preprocess it. ReElement would then refine the LFP black mass into battery-grade lithium carbonate. Under a separate memorandum of understanding, ReElement and Blackion said they would share net revenue from sales of refined materials sourced through Blackion’s network.

EMCO is building a front-end platform for aggregation, dismantling, preprocessing and conditioning that feeds downstream refining at affiliate ReElement and other partners. Where commercially appropriate, ReElement can refine battery materials from EMCO into technical- and battery-grade lithium products.

A significant focus of the combined company will be battery materials, including LFP and other chemistries, manufacturing scrap and black mass. The combined company intends to work with battery and cell manufacturers, automotive and energy-storage companies, collection and logistics providers, battery recyclers, black mass producers, critical mineral processors and refiners. LFP cells contain lower concentrations of traditionally high-value metals than certain nickel- and cobalt-bearing chemistries, so the companies say LFP recycling economics depend on efficient logistics, preprocessing, scale and the ability to recover lithium economically.

“We believe we could build many of these capabilities organically, but doing so would require additional time, management resources and execution risk. Blackion brings an experienced, entrepreneurial team with complementary capabilities that can immediately strengthen what we are already building at Electrified Materials,” said Chris Dreska, CEO of Electrified Materials.

text:
Amazon is expanding its renewable energy investments in the UK through a new Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) with energy developer Statkraft.

The agreement will support the Mossy Hill onshore wind farm near Lerwick in Shetland, Scotland, adding another project to Amazon’s growing carbon-free energy portfolio.

The investment forms part of the company’s wider approach to supporting new renewable generation while contributing to local economic activity and the UK’s energy transition.

It also builds on Amazon’s broader commitment to investing in low-carbon technologies and infrastructure across the country.

Amazon backs new Shetland wind farm

The Mossy Hill wind farm, located near Lerwick in the Shetland Islands, will generate 36 MW of renewable electricity under Amazon’s PPA.

Once operational, the project is expected to produce enough renewable electricity to power the equivalent of more than 57,000 homes each year.

Mossy Hill is expected to become operational in November 2030, adding new renewable generation to Scotland’s energy infrastructure.

The agreement gives Statkraft an anchor customer for the project while enabling Amazon to secure renewable electricity through a long-term arrangement.

“Our latest project in the Shetland Islands builds on years of investment in renewable energy across the UK," says John Boumphrey, Amazon UK and Ireland Country Manager.

"From the Shetland Islands to the coasts of England, our renewable energy investments are creating real jobs and powering local communities.

“Last year we announced our plan to invest £40bn (US$53bn) in the UK by 2027 and the transition to a lower-carbon economy is a part of how we're putting that commitment to work."

It also strengthens Amazon’s presence within Scotland’s renewable energy landscape as the company continues to expand its UK carbon-free energy portfolio.

Growing renewable energy investments

Mossy Hill adds to Amazon’s existing renewable energy investments in Scotland, including PPAs supporting the Moray West offshore wind farm in the Moray Firth and the Chirmorie Wind Farm in South Ayrshire.

These projects form part of Amazon’s wider UK portfolio, which now includes more than 50 carbon-free energy projects.

Collectively, the projects are expected to provide more than 1GW of carbon-free energy capacity across the UK.

That capacity is equivalent to enough electricity to power more than 1.3 million UK households annually.

Beyond renewable generation, Amazon’s sustainability activity in Scotland includes its Dunfermline fulfilment centre, where returned products can be assessed, repaired and resold through Amazon Resale, as well as a Glasgow micromobility hub using electric cargo bikes for last-mile deliveries.

"We're pleased to have agreed a partnership with Amazon for our Mossy Hill Wind Farm in Shetland, which gives us the certainty to move the project forward,” says Kevin O'Donovan, Statkraft's UK and Ireland Country Manager.

“Shetland has a proud history of energy production and as the country shifts towards more homegrown renewable power, we're proud to be playing our part in that transition."

Low-carbon investment supports the UK economy

Amazon’s renewable energy activity is also linked to wider investment in the UK’s low-carbon economy.

Independent analysis by Frontier Economics found that Amazon invested more than £3bn (US$3.99bn) in low-carbon technologies in the UK between 2021 and 2025.

The analysis found that these investments supported up to 34,000 jobs during the period, demonstrating the employment dimension of renewable energy and wider low-carbon infrastructure projects.

Amazon’s role as an energy purchaser through PPAs can also help provide the commercial certainty needed for renewable projects to progress from development into construction and operation.

The company’s renewable energy investments therefore sit alongside its broader UK investment plans, which include commitments to infrastructure, facilities, technology and jobs.

Renewable energy and UK energy security

Amazon’s expansion of its carbon-free energy portfolio comes as the UK seeks to increase domestic renewable generation and strengthen the resilience of its energy system.

New wind projects can contribute additional sources of electricity while supporting the development of infrastructure needed to integrate renewable power into the wider grid.

Corporate PPAs can play a role in this process by connecting large energy users with new renewable generation and providing developers with long-term demand.

Amazon’s UK approach forms part of its wider Climate Pledge commitment to reach net-zero carbon across its operations by 2040.

The company is also expanding carbon-free energy investments across Europe, positioning renewable power as a component of its longer-term decarbonisation strategy.

name: American Energy
title: Trump can't stop America's shift to clean energy. And we can accelerate it. | Leah Stokes
authors: Leah Stokes, Hannah Osborne, Tia Ghose, www.livescience.com, leah-stokes
description:
Donald Trump cannot make clean energy expensive again.
Which means that despite Trump's best efforts to prop up fossil fuels, America will transform its electricity system.
The first step is getting rid of coal, which already can't compete with clean energy.
And we know how to put up clean energy fast: the solar industry tripled its annual build rate in just six years.
Pair that with simple plug-in batteries, and ordinary people can generate and store their own clean energy at home.
text:
Donald Trump cannot make clean energy expensive again. He can only make Americans pay extra for it. His tariffs do just that. But cost declines work like a ratchet. Every solar factory built and every panel installed pushes costs down the curve. The global price floor just keeps falling.

Which means that despite Trump's best efforts to prop up fossil fuels, America will transform its electricity system. The question is how fast. And that speed is up to us.

Since 2015, most of the new power built in America has been clean. This year, 93% of new electricity capacity is expected to come from solar, wind and batteries. That is not because of any president. It is because clean energy is the cheapest way to add electricity to the grid.

The problem is what was built before. Today, 57% of America's power is generated from burning fossil fuels, compared to just 43% from clean sources. Even with solar and wind dominating new builds, our legacy system still uses dirty energy, which takes time to replace.

The first step is getting rid of coal, which already can't compete with clean energy. Coal generates about one-sixth of our power, yet 99% of American coal plants are more expensive to keep open than it would cost to replace them with new solar, wind, and storage. In Michigan, the Trump administration ordered an aging coal plant to stay open past its planned retirement. That single decision costs consumers $600,000 a day. On Sept. 11, a federal court rejected the order.

Despite Trump's attempts to revive a dying industry, the coal industry remains in deep decline – down 43% since 2010. Coal cannot compete on cost or reliability. Without expensive government welfare, coal is on its way out.

Gas plants are responsible for much of the remaining electricity emissions. Solar, wind and batteries are increasingly cost-competitive with gas. Even without subsidies, solar paired with batteries is now cheaper to build and run than a new gas plant. And we know how to put up clean energy fast: the solar industry tripled its annual build rate in just six years.

Skeptics raise two objections. First, rising electricity demand from AI, data centers and electrification means that we can't generate enough power with clean energy alone, and therefore we need to keep gas on the grid. Second, Trump's hostility — namely expiring tax credits and tariffs on solar panels and batteries — will stall the build-out.

Energy demand growth is real. Proposals for new gas plants to power data centers have surged. But more than three-quarters of this gas plant pipeline is still early stage, and many projects have been delayed. Supply backlogs on gas turbines stretch toward the 2030s. Meanwhile, new solar plants and batteries can go up in under two years. This makes building such capacity the fastest, cheapest solution to rising electricity consumption.

As for Trump: his administration won't be around forever. And rising electricity prices have become a central issue in this year's midterms. Politicians promising affordability will turn to the cheapest way to power households: clean energy. And the market will keep the transition moving no matter who's in the White House.

In the meantime, there is plenty we can do at the state and local level to speed things up. One strategy is removing barriers to plug-in solar. In Germany, more than a million households have installed "balcony solar," which are panels that plug into a wall outlet, bypassing permits or utility paperwork. Utah legalized plug-in solar last year, and California's legislature just approved it too. Pair that with simple plug-in batteries, and ordinary people can generate and store their own clean energy at home.

We can also use electric machines to soak up power when it's fossil-free. That happens in the middle of the day, when cheap solar floods the system. With the right controls, an electric water heater can also be a battery: heat the tank at noon, and tonight's shower is stored sunshine. Heat pumps can pre-cool or pre-heat a home before evening the same way. Charge electric cars at work and your commute is solar-powered.

And none of this requires the federal government. States can make midday power cheap, or even free, and pay households to shift their usage. Cities can write building codes that make flexible electric machines the default replacement. Do that at scale and we can serve growing demand with the grid we already have.

No single choice transforms the electricity system on its own. But the energy transition has always moved in waves: it dips, then surges back stronger. Millions of people pushing in the same direction is exactly how the next wave builds.

So is a clean grid realistic? Yes. The only real question is how fast we replace the old one. And that's largely up to us.

text:
A series of deadly heat waves from May to August overwhelmed Germany’s healthcare and emergency response systems and led to an estimated 16,000 heat-related deaths during the summer, the most heat mortalities ever recorded in the highly developed country.

At the 2026 Extreme Weather Congress in Hamburg this month, experts from local and regional governments, hospitals and universities said that Germany’s advanced climate research and weather technology provided accurate forecasts of persistently dangerous high temperatures, but the death toll exposed gaps between scientific knowledge and the country’s adaptation efforts, as well as shortcomings in the emergency response.

A report released during the Hamburg meeting explains that Germany’s building, cooling, water and transportation infrastructure was built for a climate that no longer exists, and that its health system is not heat-resilient. Meteorologists said heat messaging was fragmented across levels of government, while health researchers and other caregivers described hospitals’ lack of procedures for declaring and managing heat emergencies.

Across the world, accurate heat forecasts don’t translate to effective protection from its impacts, and other regions may be just one extreme heat wave away from mass casualties like Germany’s, said Kristie Ebi, a University of Washington global health professor who has helped guide major international climate reports.

In 2021, a well-forecasted heat dome over the Pacific Northwest drove temperatures far beyond previous regional records, pushing local heat resilience to the limit. More than 1,000 excess deaths and a 69-fold increase in heat-related hospitalizations followed.

Cities and counties scrambled to keep up by opening emergency cooling shelters and other pop-up measures, Ebi said, but coordinating a response across public health, emergency services and other agencies takes more than a day or two in the midst of an unfolding mass-casualty heat wave. It requires long-term planning, including “stress tests” against increasingly severe heat scenarios as greenhouse gas pollution continues to accumulate in the atmosphere.

The heat deaths in Germany and the Pacific Northwest expose a broad weakness in heat preparedness, Ebi said: Warning systems are often not designed around what happens after the alert goes out—how people receive and react to the information, who coordinates the response, how vulnerable people are contacted and who ensures that cooling centers are accessible and identified.

In England and Wales, heat-related deaths soared to at least 2,700 in May and June, marking one of the deadliest years on record, according to the UK Met Office.

Clair Barnes, a climate researcher at Imperial College London’s Centre for Environmental Policy, said understanding how people perceive and respond to risk is crucial as extreme heat becomes more common. Repeated heat waves can quickly normalize dangerous conditions. During high-level heat warnings in the United Kingdom this summer, Barnes observed people returning to their usual dog-walking and running routines.

Building effective communication, Barnes and other researchers said, requires trusted messengers in local social networks, alongside clear weather warnings linked to specific protective measures. Broad public messaging alone may not reach older people, migrant and refugee communities, people with disabilities and others who may be isolated and especially vulnerable to extreme heat.

Compounding Threats

Ebi, the University of Washington scientist, said extreme climate impacts can also collide and compound each other in ways that undermine standard heat advice. As the heat dome settled over the Pacific Northwest in 2021, wildfire smoke made it harder to cool homes by opening windows, she added, highlighting the need for cooling shelters to prepare for both extreme heat and hazardous air pollution.

At the Hamburg conference, German meteorologist Karsten Schwanke said it was a “routine work day” when he started forecasting the coming temperatures in late May.

“The 2026 heat wave was nothing that surprised us,” he said. What did surprise him was the lack of a meaningful response until the forecasted temperatures actually arrived. Official agencies appeared to wait, out of bureaucratic reticence, to see whether the heat wave would happen rather than taking a proactive approach, he said.

Schwanke said that, at the current level of human-caused warming, even hotter temperatures, exceeding 110 to 114 degrees Fahrenheit, would have been possible last summer under a slightly different atmospheric pattern.

“It won’t surprise me if that happens in the next two years sometime,” he said. What does startle him is that Germany hasn’t done more to update vulnerable infrastructure after 30 years of clear warnings.

Even today, Schwanke added, roads, schools and hospitals are often still being built according to standards developed in the 1980s. He views that as evidence that political leaders have yet to fully grasp the threat global warming can pose. Infrastructure being designed and built today needs to be resilient to temperatures that could approach 120 degrees Fahrenheit by 2050, he said.

Barnes, the UK-based climate scientist who studies how global warming affects extreme weather, said similar adaptation measures are needed in northern European cities and other temperate regions that have not experienced anything resembling today’s extreme heat in the centuries since they were built.

“We’re seeing more dangerous extreme temperatures sooner than we expected to see by this point.”

— Clair Barnes, Imperial College London’s Centre for Environmental Policy

Scientists with the UK Met Office and other researchers found that human-caused warming added between 5 and 7 degrees Fahrenheit to the maximum temperatures “and is estimated to be responsible for about 42 percent of the deaths” during heat waves in May and June.

In northern Europe, “we need to shift our attitude to accept that we are now going to have to build resilience for an extreme climate” outside the bounds of what human societies have experienced in the last few thousand years, Barnes said. Extreme heat should be treated as a systemic public health threat, much like seasonal influenza risks, not as an occasional hazard, she added.

Yet a lack of standardized heat-death reporting across jurisdictions makes it difficult to understand the scale of the threat and to prepare adequately, she said.

“It’s important to have an understanding of the historic trends to look at what we might be facing in coming years,” Barnes said. The average annual temperature increases of recent years are within the range projected by models, but, she said, “We’re seeing more dangerous extreme temperatures sooner than we expected to see by this point.”

Normalizing Heat Deaths?

Counting heat wave deaths across jurisdictions is complicated because heat can exacerbate a range of underlying conditions, said Hanns Moshammer, an environmental physician at the Medical University of Vienna.

The true toll can be obscured when death certificates list conditions such as heart failure, stroke or kidney failure rather than heat as a contributing factor. Moshammer also said that heat-related deaths can be downplayed because they often are among people whose life expectancy was already limited based on pre-existing medical conditions.

Aaron Thierry, an ecological scientist and postgraduate researcher at Cardiff University in Wales, who studies communication around climate change, warned against treating those deaths as an unavoidable consequence of extreme heat.

“That was kind of the narrative we heard around COVID, about people being disposable, and that’s not a good thing, that’s not how we should be thinking about these things at all,” he said.

Barnes recalled receiving a heartbreaking email on the day the 2025 heat-deaths analysis that she co-authored was released. The writer told her that his father had been hospitalized with heart issues but seemed to be doing well.

“He was sitting up in bed, he was chatting, he was fine,” the acquaintance wrote.

text:
HEVO, a New York-based Tier 1 supplier of wireless charging hardware and software, will work with Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) and BMW in a technology evaluation program focused on advancing next-generation wireless charging technology.

HEVO will contribute wireless charging expertise, engineering support and circular coil topologies to assist BMW’s bench testing to evaluate compatibility with ORNL’s proprietary polyphase coil technology.

The participants explain that polyphase wireless charging has the potential to improve the power density, efficiency and packaging of wireless charging systems. ORNL and BMW have publicly demonstrated advances in polyphase wireless charging systems that highlight the potential of the technology for next-gen mobility platforms.

The testing will build upon ORNL and BMW efforts to explore advanced wireless charging architectures capable of supporting future electric mobility platforms. HEVO believes wireless charging will play an increasingly important role in enabling automated vehicle operations.

“Wireless charging will be a foundational technology for the future of electric and autonomous transportation,” said Jeremy McCool, founder and CEO of HEVO. “As an ORNL technology licensee, HEVO is pleased to support the continued evaluation of circular and polyphase wireless charging systems through technical analysis. Our objective is to contribute practical experience from commercial wireless charging deployments while helping evaluate technologies that may support future EV ecosystems.”

text:
September 22, 2026

Hon. Michelle L. Phillips

Secretary to the Commission

New York State Public Service Commission

Three Empire State Plaza

Albany, NY 12223-1350

Re: Case 15-E-0302 — Comments on the Draft 2026 Clean Energy Standard Biennial Review

Dear Secretary Phillips,

As the State Senator representing the 54th Senate District, I submit these comments on the Draft 2026 Clean Energy Standard Biennial Review. I respectfully request that they be included in the official record of this proceeding.

My constituents are increasingly concerned about rising utility bills and whether New York will have the reliable, affordable energy needed to support our communities.

I hear from seniors who have worked their entire lives, paid off their homes, and now worry about whether they can afford to stay. Rising utility bills and property taxes are taking a growing share of their fixed incomes. Where will they go if the costs become more than they can manage?

Our farmers, manufacturers, and small businesses need affordable, dependable energy to operate and grow. Major investments, including the Fairlife manufacturing facility in Webster, create opportunities for our region and the dairy farmers who supply it. But those opportunities depend on reliable power and infrastructure that can support future growth.

We also need electricity to build the housing our communities desperately need. Across multiple counties in my district, housing projects have already been delayed because sufficient electric capacity was unavailable or the cost of extending service was simply too high.

The Draft Biennial Review projects significantly greater electricity demand by 2030, while expected renewable generation remains well below the state's statutory target. How much will it cost to close that gap? Who will pay for the additional generation, storage and transmission? And can New York maintain reliable service as demand continues to grow?

In July 2024, State Comptroller Thomas DiNapoli found that the costs of transitioning to renewable energy had not been reasonably estimated, leaving ratepayers as the primary identified funding source. He recommended detailed cost estimates, regular public reporting, and an assessment of how much of the financial burden ratepayers can reasonably bear.

Two years later, what has changed?

NYSERDA's February 2026 analysis of potential Climate Act compliance costs raises additional affordability concerns, particularly for Upstate households and businesses.

I ask the Commission to explain how it has addressed the Comptroller's recommendations, how NYSERDA's potential cost projections are being considered in Clean Energy Standard planning, and what additional costs ratepayers may face.

That analysis should identify the expected impact on monthly utility bills, including the costs of generation, storage, transmission, and maintaining reliable service. It should distinguish current costs from projected future costs, account for expected benefits and savings, and assess the impacts on residential, agricultural, commercial and industrial customers, particularly in the NYSEG and RG&E service territories.

I am also concerned about reliability. NYISO's 2026 Power Trends report and its reliability assessments examine growing electricity demand, generator retirements and the availability of replacement resources. As New York moves toward greater electrification, the Commission must account for the additional demand created by state mandates and ensure sufficient generation and grid infrastructure are available.

For many of my constituents, reliable electricity is more than a matter of convenience. I have heard directly from residents of senior living facilities and group homes who are concerned about losing power. An extended outage can put their health and safety at risk. It can also leave rural families without heat or running water, disrupt dairy operations and food processing, and affect emergency services.

I ask the Commission to explain how its planning aligns with NYISO's reliability assessments and accounts for existing electric capacity constraints, connection costs, and infrastructure delays that are already affecting housing and economic development in Upstate communities. Where these concerns fall outside this review, they should be addressed through appropriate utility planning and rate proceedings.

Cost allocation is equally important. Our residents and businesses should not be expected to absorb costs attributable to large new electric loads or infrastructure investments that primarily benefit other regions.

As data centers and other large electricity users seek access to New York's grid, the Commission should clearly identify who benefits from new generation and transmission investments, who is responsible for those costs, and how existing ratepayers will be affected.

Ontario, Wayne and Livingston, as well as parts of Monroe counties are home to productive farmland, important water resources and natural landscapes that contribute to our economy and quality of life.

Has the Commission quantified how many additional acres of prime agricultural soils may be affected by renewable-energy development, how much land could be removed from agricultural production, and what cumulative impacts may result for our farms and natural resources? I also ask the Commission to work with DEC to evaluate potential risks to soil and water from materials used in solar panels, including PFAS where present, and determine whether existing safeguards adequately address damaged panels and end-of-life disposal.

Opportunities to develop renewable energy on rooftops, brownfields, major parking areas, and previously disturbed sites should also be fully considered.

Local decision-making must also be considered as New York plans for additional renewable-energy development. The Office of Renewable Energy Siting and Electric Transmission (ORES) has final permitting authority over major renewable-energy projects and may override local laws. While municipalities can participate, Home Rule is ignored, and their ability to determine how projects affect their communities is significantly limited. The Commission should account for these limitations when evaluating the cumulative impacts of meeting the state's renewable-energy targets on farmland, water resources, and rural communities.

I respectfully request that the Commission address these concerns in its final Biennial Review, with a clear accounting of expected costs, reliability needs, and impacts on Upstate communities.

Sincerely,

Pamela A. Helming

Senator, 54th District

The U.S. energy storage market set a new record for energy capacity deployments in the second quarter of 2026, driven by longer system durations and expanding power demands from data center operations.
The market installed 5.4 GW of storage capacity in Q2 2026, marking a 7% year-over-year decrease in power capacity while achieving a 16% increase in total energy capacity.

The residential energy storage sector recorded a strong quarter, adding 676 MW and nearly 1.2 GWh of capacity.
Residential power capacity increased 3% year-over-year, while energy capacity jumped 48% as installers deployed larger battery systems per household.
text:
The U.S. energy storage market set a new record for energy capacity deployments in the second quarter of 2026, driven by longer system durations and expanding power demands from data center operations. According to the latest Q3 2026 U.S. Energy Storage Monitor report released by Wood Mackenzie and the American Clean Power Association, total deployments across all market segments reached 18.9 GWh, surpassing previous quarterly capacity totals.

The market installed 5.4 GW of storage capacity in Q2 2026, marking a 7% year-over-year decrease in power capacity while achieving a 16% increase in total energy capacity. The surge in energy capacity reflects an ongoing industry shift toward four-hour and longer-duration battery systems to satisfy utility adequacy requirements and localized grid constraints.

The utility-scale segment remained the primary growth driver, deploying 4.7 GW and 17.6 GWh during the second quarter. Power output fell 8% year-over-year as primary markets like California and Texas approached local grid saturation, yet energy capacity rose 16%. Total utility-scale installations for the first half of the year remained higher compared to the same period in 2025, buoyed by long-duration contracts and compliance-driven procurement.

The residential energy storage sector recorded a strong quarter, adding 676 MW and nearly 1.2 GWh of capacity. Residential power capacity increased 3% year-over-year, while energy capacity jumped 48% as installers deployed larger battery systems per household. California, Texas, Puerto Rico, Arizona, and Illinois accounted for the vast majority of residential installations. Despite positive quarterly performance, analysts project a minor full-year contraction for the residential segment in 2026, citing policy adjustments and incentive rollbacks.

The Community, Commercial, and Industrial storage sector normalized to 48 MW and 103 MWh during Q2 2026. Following elevated first-quarter activity caused by Net Energy Metering deadlines in California, non-residential installations slipped 2% year-over-year, though gains in Hawaii, New Mexico, and Texas offset domestic contraction.

Looking ahead, Wood Mackenzie withdrew its previous forecast of a near-term market contraction, citing a high volume of projects initiating construction to secure Investment Tax Credit safe harbor status. The firm projects the U.S. storage market will grow more than 50% in megawatt terms over the next five years, expanding cumulative capacity to 207 GW and 715 GWh by 2031. The utility-scale segment is expected to maintain steady growth through 2031, supported by grid interconnection developments and massive load expansion from AI data centers.

This includes concerns about the use of the judgment fund and how the Trump administration has used funds provided for an offshore wind energy program.
text:
The Trump administration’s buyouts of offshore wind leaseholders to stifle the nascent clean energy projects have drawn plenty of criticism from Democrats and environmental groups.

Now comes a new argument from a nonpartisan watchdog group: Taxpayers are taking it on the chin from the controversial lease deals — which cost the Treasury nearly $4 billion without yet demonstrating a return on the intended alternative investments in more traditional energy projects.

“The taxpayer concerns extend well beyond the cost of the buyouts themselves,” says the report from Taxpayers for Common Sense. “The buyouts return revenue already collected through competitive auctions, eliminate future lease and operating revenues, use the judgment fund to finance a major policy reversal, and steer private investment to projects in some cases handpicked by the administration.”

Since March, the Trump administration reached a dozen agreements with the leaseholders who won competitive auctions for offshore wind leases under President Joe Biden, when the Interior Department took actions to support offshore wind development.

Interior Secretary Doug Burgum has referred to these buyouts as “commonsense” actions, in part because the 2025 Republican reconciliation law curtailed tax credits for wind power that were expanded by the 2022 Democratic reconciliation law.

The administration has also been strongly critical of wind and solar energy projects since these are intermittent forms of power that do not produce the same amount of power consistently. The administration has argued wind and solar would do little to meet demand spurred largely by constantly running data centers, while their opponents have said we need all forms of energy as consumer prices continue to rise.

In total, the Interior Department has reimbursed $3.9 billion to six offshore wind developers. The funds are provided through the Treasury Department’s judgment fund, which is a permanently appropriated fund created to cover costs associated with court judgments and settlements.

These offshore wind projects had an estimated nameplate capacity of 19.2 gigawatts, the Taxpayers for Common Sense report found. The agreements came with requirements that the developers use the money to invest in other energy projects, including oil and gas production, natural gas-fired power plants, nuclear, geothermal and grid infrastructure.

The agreements do not detail how much capacity would be replaced.

‘No path forward’

For their part, the companies saw the political writing on the wall and acquiesced in part to avoid costly legal battles.

Take RWE U.S. Offshore, a unit of the German energy company that received $1.22 billion back from the government with the intent of reinvesting the funds in natural gas infrastructure, including a Louisiana liquefied natural gas facility being developed by Australia-based Woodside Energy.

“After careful consideration, it was determined there is no path forward to permit these [offshore wind] projects in the U.S. for the foreseeable future,” RWE said in a Aug. 6 statement when the deal was announced. “The company determined that this resolution best serves the interests of its stakeholders and allows it to direct resources toward energy projects that can be advanced with certainty.”

Mia Huang, a policy analyst with Taxpayers for Common Sense, said there were some concerns that these agreements do not ensure the companies use the money for new energy infrastructure. The report highlighted an agreement with the American subsidiary of TotalEnergies, which received $928 million to walk away from leases off the coast of New York and North Carolina.

When the Interior Department and TotalEnergies announced the agreement, it highlighted investment in four production units, or trains, of the Rio Grande liquefied natural gas plant in Texas. However, the company had already announced its finalized agreement for the fourth train six months prior to the wind lease buyout.

Neither TotalEnergies nor the Interior Department returned a request for comment.

“Some of this investment has already been made, so it doesn’t really add to the pool to increase the total future supply, and instead it only pulls from future supply and away from electricity that all American households can tap into in the future,” said Huang.

These buyout agreements have triggered strong opposition from Democrats across the country. Nine Democratic state attorneys general have filed multiple lawsuits challenging these agreements, arguing that the administration improperly used the judgment fund and violated laws including the Administrative Procedure Act and Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act.

At a Sept. 17 press conference, Rep. Chellie Pingree, D-Maine, criticized the agreements and said the Trump administration reversed course while “on a pathway to bringing down energy costs.”

“They took taxpayer dollars that were being invested in important projects that would have brought down the cost of energy for all of us and our communities, and they paid bribes and they paid out to utility companies to get them to turn in the opposite direction,” said Pingree.

Pingree, who’s currently ranking member of the House Interior-Environment Appropriations Subcommittee, added that if she were to get the gavel in the next Congress, the panel would investigate these deals.

Pingree spokesperson Gabrielle Mannino said that this oversight would include questions for Burgum from House Democrats about the agreements that have gone unanswered. This includes concerns about the use of the judgment fund and how the Trump administration has used funds provided for an offshore wind energy program.

In the Senate, 14 Democratic caucus members, including Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., and Energy and Natural Resources ranking member Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., have also pressed the energy companies involved in the agreements for additional answers.

text:
Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...

An East Texas coal-fired power plant has been given another lease on life thanks to the Trump administration’s repeal of certain environmental regulations.

The Environmental Protection Agency is repealing regulations requiring coal-fired power plants to close if they don’t reduce greenhouse gas emissions within the coming years.

Agency leaders announced the changes Sept. 14 as part of President Donald Trump’s plan to “unleash American energy.” The agency also plans to eliminate all additional regulations aimed at reducing greenhouse gas emissions in the power sector, EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin said.

The regulatory rollbacks mean coal-fired power plants such as Martin Lake plant near Tatum won’t be forced to close or comply with certain costly emissions reduction measures within the next decade.

Leaders of the Sierra Club, a traditionally left-leaning environmental advocacy firm, said the rollback is a detriment to public health, as climate change, premature deaths and asthma cases are tied to higher emissions of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases from coal-fired and natural gas-fired power plants.

Trump administration officials and organizations on the political right, however, say the rollbacks don’t have a negative impact on human health, and their elimination will lower energy costs for everyday Americans. Leaders of the traditionally right-leaning Heartland Institute said that increased greenhouse gas emissions have positive impacts on vegetation worldwide.

Leaders of Vistra, the parent company of plant owner Luminant, did not respond to a request for comment.

‘More prosperous America’

The Obama and Biden administrations made greenhouse gas reductions core parts of the EPA’s plan to combat climate change. The Trump administration, however, has sought to deregulate the energy industry, with the president saying climate change is a “con job.”

EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin announced the rollback Sept. 14 in Houston, saying it will promote electric grid reliability by protecting coal-fired power generation. He also said it will save American electric customers and electric businesses $310 billion, though he didn’t give a timeline for those savings. Officials said they estimate coal production for use in the power sector to increase by 10 times.

“For over 15 years, the Obama and Biden administrations implemented a war on coal to destroy reliable and affordable energy. The Trump administration has come in to protect American energy and to make sure you can afford to keep the lights on,” Zeldin said in a statement. “Americans will see a decrease in electricity prices, but this is just the beginning. We are working to go even further so that American energy can be fully unleashed. Realizing the full potential of American energy means more jobs, lower prices, and a more prosperous America.”

While Zeldin said the rollback will lower energy prices, Sierra Club leaders disagree. Studies show that green energy is cleaner, cheaper to produce and more reliable than coal-fired power generation.

“The coal industry cannot compete with solar – it’s being kept on life support by taxpayer subsidies and regulatory handouts, while ordinary families pay the price in higher electricity bills, dirtier air, and more extreme weather fueled by carbon pollution,” Sierra Club leaders said in a statement.

Public health concerns debated

Central to the debate over greenhouse gas emissions is whether they negatively impact human and environmental health.

Power generation facilities are the nation’s second-largest emitters of greenhouse gases, with transportation as the largest contributor, according to the EPA. Greenhouse gas emissions trap heat and make the plant warmer, the agency’s website states.

The U.S. is the world’s second-largest emitter of carbon dioxide. The largest producer, China, emits 13 billion tons of carbon dioxide annually, and the U.S. emits 4.6 billion tons.

Texas coal and natural gas plants emitted 190 million tons of carbon in 2025, according to EPA data.

Jaime Perkins, a campaign organizer with the Sierra Club, said greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide warm the planet and contribute to natural disasters, and they can contribute to health issues, such as asthma, heart attacks and lung issues.

Those assertions are affirmed by organizations such as the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

With the rollback, power plants are “left off the hook” from changes that would have prevented and reduced health issues in area residents, Perkins said.

The impact of the regulatory rollback extends beyond carbon reduction. Sierra Club leaders said the carbon reductions also would have reduced emissions of mercury, heavy metals, particulate matter, nitrogen oxides and sulfur dioxide.

Martin Lake is one of the top four pollution-emitting power plants in Texas, Sierra Club officials have stated, based on publicly available pollution data.

The Clean Air Task Force, a global nonprofit that aims to eliminate carbon from the energy sector, estimates that pollution from Martin Lake contributes to dozens of premature deaths, heart attacks, asthma cases and more in people living near the plant.

Zeldin and other EPA officials disagree with concerns about greenhouse gases. In the Sept. 14 press release, Zeldin said the gases targeted by the regulations — and any public health concerns related to them — “are too uncertain, conjectural, remote, and convoluted to tie specifically to the U.S. power sector.”

Leaders of the Heartland Institute also say they believe higher carbon dioxide emissions can yield benefits to the planet. Anthony Watts, a senior fellow at the institute, said Sept. 14 that rising levels of carbon dioxide have “well-documented benefits.” For example, they’ve contributed to higher plant growth and made crops more productive.

“If power-plant CO2 emissions are supposedly destroying the planet, a greener Earth with enhanced plant growth is an inconvenient fact that deserves far more attention,” Watts said. “Any rational assessment of CO2 regulation should consider these measurable benefits alongside its claimed costs.”

The EPA’s regulatory rollbacks are expected to face legal challenges.

text:
Mercedes-Benz is taking another step toward next-generation electric vehicle batteries after signing a joint testing agreement with ProLogium Holding Inc. The agreement gives Mercedes-Benz priority access to ProLogium’s latest Gen4 battery cells for extensive testing as the automaker evaluates advanced battery technology for future EV applications.

The partnership builds on nearly a decade of cooperation between Mercedes-Benz and ProLogium, which has included battery development, validation and testing of multiple cell formats and technologies.

Under the new agreement, ProLogium’s Gen4 battery technology will undergo electrical, thermal and safety testing at Mercedes-Benz facilities as well as specialized independent testing institutes. The testing is expected to provide Mercedes-Benz with data needed to determine whether the new battery technology could eventually be integrated into future electric vehicles.

ProLogium Gen4 Battery Targets Higher Energy Density and Faster Charging

ProLogium’s Gen4 battery platform is designed around five key objectives: intrinsic safety, high performance, increased energy density, scalable production and a competitive cost structure.

The battery architecture uses a non-flammable inorganic electrolyte and ceramic separator technology. ProLogium also incorporates its proprietary active safety mechanism, which is intended to improve the overall safety characteristics of the cells.

Alongside safety improvements, the Gen4 technology is being developed to deliver fast charging, high power output and improved performance in low-temperature conditions. These characteristics could be particularly important as automakers continue working to reduce charging times while increasing EV range and performance.

ProLogium says its approach is designed to move advanced battery technology beyond laboratory development and toward large-scale commercial production.

“Over nearly a decade, our collaboration with Mercedes-Benz has evolved from early cell development and validation to testing our latest Gen4 technology for future vehicle applications,” said Vincent Yang, founder and CEO of ProLogium.

Yang added that the company is focused on turning years of battery development into scalable manufacturing and commercially viable products, with its European expansion supported by Mercedes-Benz as well as the French government and European Union.

Mercedes-Benz and ProLogium Have Worked Together Since 2016

The relationship between the two companies dates back to 2016. Since then, their collaboration has expanded from early hybrid-solid-state Gen3 battery development and joint validation toward potential applications in future vehicle platforms.

Mercedes-Benz has become a long-term global automotive partner and strategic investor in ProLogium. The German automaker has also supported the development and validation of several lithium ceramic battery formats, including pouch cells, next-generation prismatic cells and ProLogium’s Bi-Polar technology.

Jörg Burzer, member of the Board of Management of Mercedes-Benz Group AG and chief technology officer for development and procurement, said the partnership combines ProLogium’s solid-state battery technology with Mercedes-Benz’s expertise in battery development, testing and vehicle integration.

The latest testing agreement therefore represents another stage in a partnership that has increasingly focused on technologies that could be used in future electric vehicles.

ProLogium Expands Battery Manufacturing in Europe

Large-scale manufacturing is a key part of ProLogium’s strategy. The company’s Taoke Gigafactory in Taiwan has completed GWh-scale manufacturing validation and supports C-sample production, demonstration vehicle programs and future commercial production.

In Europe, ProLogium is developing a planned gigafactory in Dunkirk, France. The facility is expected to eventually have production capacity of up to 44 GWh, providing localized battery manufacturing and supply-chain capabilities for European customers.

The Dunkirk facility is intended to replicate the production model established in Taiwan. Once its first phase is completed, ProLogium expects to have the capacity to supply commercial battery cells to European automakers at a scale suitable for electric vehicle platforms.

Mercedes-Benz is also represented on ProLogium’s Board of Directors and has expressed support for the company’s Dunkirk development plans. ProLogium is additionally planning a potential NASDAQ listing in the fourth quarter of 2026.

What the Gen4 Battery Could Mean for Future Mercedes EVs

The latest agreement does not confirm that ProLogium’s Gen4 cells will be used in a production Mercedes-Benz EV. The technology must first complete Mercedes-Benz’s electrical, thermal and safety evaluation before its suitability for future vehicle applications can be determined.

However, the testing highlights the growing importance of advanced battery technology as Mercedes-Benz continues developing its next generation of electric vehicles.

If ProLogium’s Gen4 cells meet the automaker’s requirements, the combination of high energy density, fast charging, high power output, low-temperature performance and safety-focused cell architecture could make the technology a candidate for future EV platforms.

For ProLogium, the agreement also represents an important step in moving its solid-state battery technology closer to automotive-scale commercialization, particularly as the company prepares to expand production in Europe.

General Motors is severely scaling back production plans for the reintroduced Chevrolet Bolt. Internal United Auto Workers (UAW) union documents obtained by Reuters reveal that the Kansas facility building the electric crossover is now targeting a total run of just 35,000 units-a drastic 75-percent drop from original plant capacity projections of 150,000 vehicles.

The revived 2027 Bolt, built at GM's Fairfax Assembly plant in Kansas City, Kansas, was always intended as a bridge model built on an updated version of the previous Bolt EUV platform. However, the revised production target indicates a far shorter lifespan than anticipated.

Reengineering a vehicle and re-establishing its supply chain for a meager 35,000-unit run represents an unusually low return on development capital. Analysts attribute the steep reduction to tapering consumer appetite for entry-level EVs, compounded by stiffer competition across the compact electric segment.

The federal government's recent easing of Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) standards reduced the regulatory pressure on legacy automakers to build high-volume electric vehicles strictly to offset internal combustion engine emissions averages.

In a statement responding to the report, a Chevrolet representative declined to verify specific production targets, noting that GM continuously evaluates market dynamics and customer demand to adjust operational plans.

With the Bolt's production window drawing to a close sooner than expected, GM will pivot capacity at the Fairfax plant toward higher-margin, internal-combustion offerings-including U.S. assembly of the gas-powered Chevrolet Equinox and newly migrated Buick Envision.

description:
For communities along the Gulf Coast, hurricane season presents a recurring challenge: knowing when, where and how to evacuate before a major storm hits.
To tackle this, researchers at Texas A&M University have spent more than a decade helping local, state and federal agencies develop clear, data-driven evacuation strategies.
These organizations evaluate storm surge risks and establish evacuation zones tailored to shifting coastal populations.

text:
For communities along the Gulf Coast, hurricane season presents a recurring challenge: knowing when, where and how to evacuate before a major storm hits. To tackle this, researchers at Texas A&M University have spent more than a decade helping local, state and federal agencies develop clear, data-driven evacuation strategies.

Walter Peacock, professor and principal investigator, said the research team collaborates with municipalities, county officials and federal partners that include NOAA, FEMA and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. These organizations evaluate storm surge risks and establish evacuation zones tailored to shifting coastal populations.

“We work with local counties and municipalities to re-evaluate their surge risk,” Peacock said. “We look at where inundations are likely to be given different types of storms, different trajectories, forward speeds and wind speeds. This data helps them develop their evacuation zones.”

Solving problems before they happen

The team’s efforts span coastal regions across Texas, including the Rio Grande Valley, the Coastal Bend and Southeast Texas. Through these projects, researchers examine population vulnerabilities, mapped structures and transportation logistics. The resulting data feeds directly into HURREVAC (HURRicane EVACuation), the primary software decision-makers use during active storm threats to calculate evacuation times and set emergency plans into motion.

“We take a storm that’s coming in, its forward speed, its trajectory and run a quick analysis of where it’s likely to impact,” Peacock said. “On the basis of that, they use what we’ve done for them to say, ‘OK, we probably need to evacuate zones A, B and C.’”

A major factor in evacuation planning involves human behavior and how residents respond to emergency notifications. David Bierling of the Texas A&M Transportation Institute (TTI) and the Hazard Reduction and Recovery Center’s director of transportation research leads the team’s behavioral studies and convened an analysis summit as part of the final Southeast Texas Study Area. It was attended by top evacuation researchers that have studied multiple evacuation events in Texas.

“Spatial analysis and GIS mapping allow us to pinpoint the most at-risk neighborhoods and visualize how evacuation routes interact with vulnerable populations,” said Douglas Wunneburger, co-principal investigator from the Department of Landscape Architecture and Urban Planning. “Spatial analysis steps begin with surge models based on historic and predicted storm scenarios to determine risk defined by potential maximum extent of surge inundation. The team selects well-known geographic features, usually highways, to set draft zone boundaries encompassing maximum surge extent for review by local experts and stakeholders. Once boundaries are set, estimates for population and household vulnerability factors, for number of vehicles and for temporary lodging populations are derived to feed transportation models.”

Teaming up to plan routes for evacuation

Transportation modeling plays a central role in answering these behavioral questions and mapping out realistic evacuation timelines.

Darrell Borchardt, co-PI from the TTI, said the purpose of the modeling was to provide a reasonable estimate of evacuation clearance times from the region. The Real-time Evacuation Planning Model (RTEPM) was used to evaluate each of the 88 scenarios; the set of scenarios was jointly developed by the project team in conjunction with representatives of the public agencies throughout the region. The resulting matrix of evacuation time estimates is included in HURREVAC, which is used by local officials to better plan for evacuations from their respective regions in the event of a projected landfall of a tropical system.

He said the most powerful part of the project was a combination of working with the project team as well as being in the same room with emergency managers throughout the region observing how they worked together in developing the scenarios as a group.

“Everyone involved had the same goal of facilitating evacuation throughout the region in the best interest of citizens that may be impacted by an approaching storm,” Borchardt said.

Ultimately, the initiative relies on interdisciplinary collaboration across Texas A&M departments and research institutes to deliver practical tools directly to emergency managers.

“We’re a big team effort, so we want that to continue,” Peacock said.

text:
PRESS RELEASE

September 30, 2026

Contact:

Charissee Ridgeway at EPN, charissee.ridgeway@environmentalprotectionnetwork.org, + 1 859-771-5568

Ashley Siefert Nunes at UCS, asiefert@ucs.org, +1 952-239-0199

Former EPA Children’s Health Advisers Call Out Trump Administration’s Unfulfilled Promise to Keep Kids Safe

Ahead of Children’s Health Month, experts warn EPA is weakening safeguards against toxic pollution while leaving children’s health advisory committee spots vacant

WASHINGTON — Ahead of Children’s Health Month this October, former members of the Children’s Health Protection Advisory Committee (CHPAC) are calling out the Trump administration for failing to fulfill its own commitment to engage experts in protecting children’s health.

More than 70 signatories, including more than two dozen former CHPAC members and subject-matter experts, joined by the American Academy of Pediatrics, Alliance of Nurses for Healthy Environments and others, sent a letter today urging the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to appoint and convene a scientifically credible, varied and balanced committee. In its own children’s health strategy document, the administration committed to using CHPAC as part of its effort to address environmental threats to children’s health, including efforts to address children’s exposure to chemicals, air pollution, contaminated water, and microplastics associated with chronic disease and cancer risks. Yet as MAHA leaders gather in Washington this week, EPA has left the committee partially unseated, failing to meet its promise and depriving the agency of independent, science-based guidance on protecting children from pollution and toxic chemicals when families need it most.

For nearly three decades under both Republican and Democratic administrations, CHPAC has served as an expert-led, policy-oriented network of volunteers that provides EPA with evidence-based recommendations on children’s environmental health. Its members have included independent researchers, academic experts, health care providers, scientists, and public servants in state and Tribal governments.

EPA solicited nominations in August 2025, and said it expected to fill the vacancies by March 1, 2026. However, it is seven months later and those spots remain empty, leaving the committee not fully seated and thus unable to meet. This marks a break even from the first Trump administration, which maintained a functioning CHPAC and convened it repeatedly.

“EPA is making decisions right now about pollution and toxic chemicals that can shape a child’s health for a lifetime,” said Jeanne Briskin, former Director of EPA’s Office of Children’s Health Protection. “For nearly three decades, CHPAC has given EPA concrete recommendations on protecting children from lead, pesticides, PFAS, air pollution and other hazards. The administration cannot credibly promise to deliver on its children’s health strategy while leaving this expert committee vacant.”

The letter calls on EPA to take three steps by November 1, 2026:

Set a Clear Timeline: Announce when EPA will appoint and convene a scientifically credible, varied and balanced CHPAC.

Respond to Past Plastics Recommendations: Provide a written response to CHPAC’s November 2025 recommendations on plastics and children’s health.

Meet with Health Experts: Convene EPA leadership and health experts to discuss integrating CHPAC’s proactive goals with the administration’s children’s health priorities.

These vacancies are especially noticeable given EPA has also repealed requirements limiting mercury and particulate pollution from coal-fired power plants and proposed eliminating federal drinking-water standards for several PFAS, which could leave children increasingly exposed to pollutants linked to neurological, respiratory, developmental, immune-system, and other serious health harms in children.

The Environmental Protection Network (EPN) and the Union of Concerned Scientists (UCS) helped organize the experts behind today’s letter. Both organizations have worked to defend the role of independent scientific advice in EPA decision-making. After the first Trump administration dismissed members of the Clean Air Scientific Advisory Committee and disbanded its particulate-pollution panel, UCS brought the experts together to convene independently and delivered their consensus recommendations directly to the EPA.

###

ABOUT THE ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION NETWORK

The Environmental Protection Network is a nonpartisan organization comprising more than 800 former EPA scientists, toxicologists, chemists, biologists, engineers, and policy analysts—many of whom spent decades as career experts inside the agency. They assessed cancer and developmental risks, studied links between pollution, fertility, and chronic disease, investigated contaminated communities, and brought enforcement actions to hold corporate polluters accountable. EPN was founded in 2017 to serve as an independent voice promoting science-based policies that protect families’ health.

South Carolina is preparing for the next phase of nuclear energy growth by expanding efforts to train workers for the industry.

The state’s third annual Nuclear Summit held in Columbia earlier this week highlighted South Carolina’s position as a national leader in nuclear power and the need to develop a skilled workforce to support future projects.

According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, South Carolina ranks third nationally in nuclear energy production. Nuclear power currently provides about 54% of the state’s electricity.

A major announcement at the summit involved a new partnership between Westinghouse Electric and the University of South Carolina aimed at preparing the next generation of nuclear workers.

The partnership plans to establish a nuclear innovation center featuring hands-on training laboratories and advanced reactor simulators. The initiative is designed to provide students and workers with practical experience as demand for nuclear expertise increases.

The effort comes as South Carolina officials seek to expand the state’s role in the nuclear industry, including the development and deployment of advanced nuclear technologies.

Federal Department of Energy officials also emphasized the growing national focus on nuclear energy and the need for collaboration among government, universities and industry.

The partnership could help create high-paying jobs while strengthening South Carolina’s workforce and supporting the state’s efforts to become a major national center for nuclear energy development.

text:
IONNA, the electric vehicle charging network established by eight car manufacturers, now operates over 180 charging sites in the United States, which is more than twice the number it had at the beginning of 2026.

The company, based in Durham, North Carolina, is launching a council of well-known electric-vehicle reviewers to feed driver complaints back into network management.

Growth in this area came after JD Power’s 2026 study of public charging was published in August, in which IONNA obtained the highest score with 807 points out of a possible 1,000, beating the Mercedes-Benz Charging Network, which had 797, and the Rivian Adventure Network, which had 755; this was IONNA’s first year of eligibility.

The network is owned by BMW, GM, Honda, Hyundai, Kia, Mercedes-Benz, Stellantis, and Toyota, and IONNA currently operates the largest network in the United States consisting of 400kW chargers.

A large portion of the recent expansion has come through convenience stores; since announcing a partnership with Circle K in April, IONNA has opened over 40 charging stations in its stores and says usage at those sites has doubled since it took over operations.

IONNA has not developed its own app and instead uses platforms that drivers are already familiar with. The number of apps included has now increased to 19 thanks to new integrations with Presto, ChargeHub, and EV Connect.

Volvo drivers will be able to begin a session using Plug & Charge, a feature that allows the car to identify itself to the charger, and support for Toyota and Lexus is due in October.

Discounts for owners are also extending to include Hyundai and Mercedes-Benz customers, who can now get cheaper charging via their car manufacturers’ apps and the Plug & Charge system, joining BMW and GM, and IONNA says that its other founding brands will do the same.

The Driver Advisory Council, consisting of Kyle Conner from the YouTube channel Out of Spec and Tom Moloughney from State of Charge, has its first job as being the testing of a new Driver’s Dashboard, this allowing live session details to be displayed in a browser without the need for an app, login, or subscription.

Seth Cutler, CEO of IONNA, stated that the industry has regarded charging scale and charging quality as a tradeoff. However, he added that the network’s growth and its satisfaction rating indicate that drivers can expect both.

The long-term aim is far greater; when IONNA started up in 2024, it said it intended to have at least 30,000 chargers installed across North America by the end of the decade.

text:
NEW JERSEY - Clean Water Action, a national organization with an active presence in the Garden State since 1982, is working in pivotal mid-term federal races across the country to both retain pro-environmental champions like Congressman Frank Pallone (CD6-NJ), as well as flip seats in Congress to be pro-environment with challenger candidates like Rebecca Bennett (CD7-NJ).

New Jersey has long led the way in setting a high bar for environmental and public health safeguards. This has resulted in the adoption of federal policies like the Superfund for toxic site cleanups, stricter drinking water standards, and so much more. Over the last two years, our accomplishments have been eroded by draconian federal rollbacks in policy, funding and staff.

Changing the make-up and voices in Congress is one of the best ways to slow down the dismantlement of vital agencies, like the US Environmental Protection Agency, and erosion of democracy as we know it in this country. Our ability to do this starts with exercising our voting rights – knowing how, when and where to vote.

This summer was a wakeup call for action - extreme heat, flash floods, loss of lives, homes, and businesses left no part of the state untouched by devastation. We are in an economic and environmental crisis that will only intensify over time and with greater frequency. Sending a strong pro-environmental majority from our NJ delegation to Washington is one way of helping to turn the tide of national policy towards protecting, not abandoning, our struggling families and economy. Becoming informed about NJ’s congressional candidates is key to making the right choices at the ballot box.

To that end, Clean Water Action is proudly supporting nine congressional candidates from New Jersey including: US Senator Cory Booker, Herb Conaway MD (CD3), Frank Pallone (CD6), Rebecca Bennett (CD7), Robert Menendez Jr. (CD8), Nellie Pou (CD9), LaMonica McIver (CD10), Analilia Mejia (CD11) and Dr. Adam Hamawy (CD12).

Below are selected quotes from Clean Water Action’s endorsed NJ candidates for Congress:

U.S. Senator Cory Booker

“I am thrilled to have the endorsement of Clean Water Action. Protecting our environment and our water has been central to my work since my time on the Newark City Council, as Mayor, and as New Jersey’s Senator. I was proud to help secure $100 million to get lead out of Newark’s drinking water and stand up to Donald Trump’s efforts to roll back environmental protections hurting New Jersey. In the Senate, I’ll continue to partner with Clean Water Action to deliver for New Jersey families feeling the worst impacts of climate change.”

CD 3 - Herb Conaway MD

"It is an honor to be endorsed by Clean Water Action, an organization that champions impactful, common-sense policies and candidates who fight to protect public health and our environment across the country.

As a physician, I have seen firsthand how the health of our environment directly impacts health outcomes in our communities. Now more than ever, as we face an administration that too often disregards science and facts, we must do everything we can to protect our natural resources and ensure every community has access to clean air, clean water, and a healthy environment."

CD 6 – Frank Pallone

“I am honored to be endorsed by Clean Water Action, which has fought to protect our rivers, lakes, and oceans for over fifty years. In our collective fight against corporate polluters who refuse to pay for the damage they cause, we need voices willing to stand up to anyone in defense of our planet. I will always use my voice to defend the environment against any attack.”

CD 7 – Rebecca Bennett

“I am excited to earn the endorsement of Clean Water Action in this race. As a mom to two daughters, I believe all of our kids should be able to grow up with access to safe, clean drinking water and outdoor space. In Congress, I’ll work to bring home federal funding to replace aging lead pipes, remove PFAS “forever chemical” contamination from our environment, and clean up Superfund sites that continue to harm our communities.”

CD 8 - Robert Menendez Jr.

"Every family deserves safe, clean drinking water. That is exactly what I am fighting for whether its by opposing Republican efforts to gut the Clean Water Act, holding AI data center companies accountable for their environmental impact, or securing millions to replace lead service lines. I am grateful to Clean Water Action for their partnership in this fight and proud to have their support as we keep working to protect the water our communities depend on."

CD 9 - Nellie Pou

"I am honored to have the support of Clean Water Action and proud to stand with an organization that has fought for decades to protect Americans' water and public health. In Congress, I have prioritized water issues and worked hard to bring federal resources home for safer drinking water, stronger wastewater systems and flood protection. Clean water is fundamental to healthy families and strong communities, and I will keep fighting to protect it across New Jersey," said Congresswoman Nellie Pou.

CD 10 - LaMonica McIver

“I am grateful to be endorsed by Clean Water Action. During my first full term in Congress I have fought to make sure that everyone in New Jersey, and across the country, has access to what they need to live a healthy life. Protecting our planet goes hand in hand with protecting our communities and delivering justice—no matter your ZIP code. At a time when so many people in power have forgotten about communities like mine, I am glad to be fighting shoulder to shoulder with the leaders at Clean Water Action to deliver what people deserve and what our planet needs.”

CD 11- Analilia Mejia

"Now more than ever, we need people-powered movements fighting for our right to clean water, clean air, and a livable planet. Protecting the water we drink, the air we breathe, and the communities we call home must be a priority. As an organizer, I know firsthand that real change happens when everyday people come together, organize, and demand better. That’s the kind of movement Clean Water Action is building, and I’m proud to have their endorsement."

CD 12 - Dr. Adam Hamawy

"A cleaner environment in New Jersey means healthier New Jerseyans. As a physician, I see the impacts of toxic pollution all the time. I am proud to earn the support of Clean Water Action and look forward to fighting together for the environment we deserve."
